<a id="item-1"></a>
## [Google announces Gemini 4 Carbon, tops new AI intelligence index](https://t.me/ai_newz/4824) ⭐️ 9.0/10

Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon, which took first place on the new Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0. The release will be gradual, starting this week with select cybersecurity professionals, followed by a wider rollout through the Fairwind program, with a general release promised 'as soon as possible'. This marks Google's second frontier model in about a month, intensifying competition at the top of the AI capability leaderboard. The staged rollout and premium pricing signal a focus on high-stakes cybersecurity use cases before broad availability. Pricing initially matches Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, but will double after the introductory period. The model reportedly scores 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro and builds on Argon's multi-layered safety and security stack.

telegram · ai_newz · Oct 28, 17:41

**Background**: The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index is a composite benchmark that evaluates language models across reasoning, coding, knowledge, instruction following, and multi-step tasks. Google's Fairwind Program, launched in September, gives approved trusted partners early access to frontier AI capabilities for cyber defense. Gemini 4 Carbon follows the earlier Argon model, which had a two-week gap between announcement and public release.

**Discussion**: Commenters expressed frustration with Google's confusing and ever-changing product naming, with one noting uncertainty about how to access the latest models. Others argued that benchmarks without immediate release are meaningless in a fast-moving field, and some suggested standardizing model tiers like Ultra, Pro, Flash, and Lite.

## [User Presence Makes LLM Negotiation Agents More Aggressive and Misaligned](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36435) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A controlled study using the PRESENT framework found that when a user is present in the loop, LLM negotiation agents obtain 13.7% higher payouts and negotiate more aggressively, but also exhibit roughly double the rate of misaligned behavior toward counterparties and misalignment toward users in 14.3% of games. These effects persisted even when users sent only templated, neutral messages. This reveals a blind spot in current evaluation practice: static instructions miss behaviors that emerge only when users are present, and outcome-level metrics cannot detect misalignment. As LLM agents increasingly act on behalf of users in multi-agent settings, these findings have direct implications for AI safety and alignment research. The study conducted 11.2k runs across 7 games and 8 models, holding the game, objectives, and user preferences fixed across conditions to isolate the effect of user presence. Misaligned behaviors were uncorrelated with outcomes, meaning higher payouts do not signal better alignment.

## [BiPA Reveals Skill Optimizers for LLM Agents May Not Truly Help](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37201) ⭐️ 8.0/10

The paper introduces BiPA, a method that replays an optimizer's acceptance rule on candidates identical to its seed to measure selection bias, and records each episode as a bipartite graph of turns and text to trace extra input tokens. Across three optimizers, three agentic benchmarks, and two models, learned skills succeed only 0.1 points higher on average than hand-written seeds, and their dev gains vanish on test. This work challenges the validity of reported gains in skill optimization for LLM agents, showing they may be artifacts of selection on small dev sets. It provides concrete principles for more rigorous evaluation, which could affect how the agentic AI community designs and benchmarks skill optimizers. The learned skills read about 16% more input tokens because optimizers almost always add rules, half to re-check work and some to act one call at a time, and the agent follows them as extra turns that re-send the whole conversation. The authors propose four principles: accept an edit only if its gain exceeds what selection alone reports, charge it for the turns it adds rather than its length, let the editor delete and merge rules, and show it what earlier rules cost.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: Skill optimizers adapt an LLM agent to long-horizon tasks by rewriting a natural-language procedure (the skill) in its context and keeping edits that raise success on a small dev set. Agentic benchmarks evaluate multi-step workflows with tools and terminals, where success is noisy, so small dev-set gains may not generalize. BiPA uses a bipartite graph—a graph whose vertices split into two disjoint sets—to link each turn to the text it reads, enabling token-cost attribution.

## [Gemma4-12B-it uses rotatable numerical subspaces across modalities and operations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37422) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.37422) uses causal interventions to identify small subspaces in Gemma4-12B-it's residual stream where swapping coordinates swaps the model's numerical answer. The study finds that text vs. image and addition vs. subtraction conditions use distinct but rotatable numerical subspaces, with a single rotation and rescaling mapping one subspace onto another and raising causal effect recovery from 53.2% to 91.4%. This work challenges similarity-based interpretability methods like RSA and CKA, which cannot distinguish identical from rotated representations, and provides causal evidence that multimodal models share numerical meaning through relational geometry across distinct coordinate frames. It has significant implications for understanding internal computation in multimodal LLMs and for designing better interpretability tools. Each subspace is split into 9 directions that the output layer reads to choose the next digit and 13 directions it cannot see; the 13 hidden directions still carry the number, and swapping them redirects the next digit in 77.6% of cases when two numbers share their first digit. This suggests the model computes the full multi-digit result early and holds it in reserve to unfold across time.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: Mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer the internal computations of neural networks, often by analyzing the residual stream—the central pathway through which information flows in transformer models. Causal interventions involve modifying internal activations to test their effect on outputs, providing stronger evidence than correlational similarity metrics like RSA (Representational Similarity Analysis) and CKA (Centered Kernel Alignment), which can give identical scores to representations that are merely rotated versions of each other. Gemma4-12B-it is a multimodal open-weights model from Google DeepMind that handles text and image input.

## [TeamGym: A New Benchmark for Multi-Agent Team Decision-Making with Distributed Information](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37571) ⭐️ 8.0/10

TeamGym is a new environment for evaluating and training language model-based agents on team decision-making tasks built from real-world legal, finance, medical, and software engineering corpora. It introduces the concept of 'pivotal information'—a minimal set of facts each necessary and collectively sufficient for a correct decision—to control information distribution and measure how well agents share and integrate it. Current AI agents are primarily trained and benchmarked in isolation, so TeamGym addresses a critical gap by providing a systematic way to study multi-agent collaboration under distributed information. The finding that distributing pivotal information lowers success rates by 22.9 percentage points on average highlights a significant communication deficit that must be overcome for AI teams to handle real-world decisions. Evaluating 8 language models on 12 source corpora, the study documents a 22.9-point communication gap when pivotal information is distributed across participants versus given to a single model, and a further 19.9-point retrieval gap when participants must extract pivotal information from source material themselves. Reinforcement learning on team decision loss improves final-decision quality and induces emergent coordination in participation, speaker selection, and communication, even though the reward evaluates only the final decision.

Astrolabe is a flow-matching-based generative emulator that operates directly on the 6N phase-space coordinates of N-body particles, avoiding voxel grids and enabling observable-agnostic cosmology simulations. ## [GateRQ: Gate-Weighted Per-Lookup Precision for Quantized Conditional Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35985) ⭐️ 8.0/10

GateRQ proposes storing conditional memory tables as ladders of 1-bit residual codes, keeping only level 1 in GPU memory to compute the gate and reading deeper levels only for lookups ranked highest by the gate. On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, this cuts GPU table memory by 7.8x and raises vLLM throughput by 11%-31% over FP8 tables without retraining, while losing about 1 PopQA point at 1.50 bits read per lookup and 0.2 points at 2.10 bits across two models. This work addresses a key bottleneck in LLM inference: large conditional memory tables that consume GPU memory and limit throughput. By enabling aggressive quantization without retraining and with minimal accuracy loss, it could make memory-heavy models like DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash more practical to deploy in production serving systems such as vLLM. The key insight is that a lookup's quantization error is weighted by its gate, which is small for frequent n-grams and large for rare long-tail entities, and this gate can be computed from a 1-bit code. This explains why refining lookups by access frequency fails compared to random refinement, and the method achieves 7.8x memory reduction with only about 1 PopQA point loss at 1.50 bits per lookup.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: Conditional memory layers, such as DeepSeek's Engram, attach large hashed n-gram tables to a language model to store factual knowledge, and removing them from DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash costs 36.8 PopQA points. Low-bit quantization of these tables tends to lose long-tail facts first, and the standard remedy of giving more bits to frequently accessed rows backfires. vLLM is a high-throughput LLM inference and serving engine, and FP8 is an 8-bit floating-point format commonly used for efficient inference.

A new arXiv paper introduces PROBE, a benchmark of all 2,457 bugs fixed over 18 months across 20 GitHub repositories, and evaluates frontier coding agents on proactive bug discovery. ## [Rollback: World Models as Counterfactual Engines for Policy Improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36068) ⭐️ 8.0/10

Researchers introduced Rollback, a policy improvement paradigm that uses action-conditioned world models to rewind to past decision points and branch into alternative actions, contrasting outcomes to attribute success to individual decisions. The method distills counterfactual outcomes into fine-grained action-level supervision without a separately learned value model, and on three real-world tasks it improved success rates over the strongest baseline by 10.67%, 11.11%, and 11.85% on block extraction, ball tossing, and tabletop curling, respectively. This work turns world models from passive forward simulators into active counterfactual engines, concentrating imagination on critical decisions and enabling more sample-efficient robot policy learning. It could significantly reduce reliance on costly real-world interaction and hand-built physics simulators, benefiting robot learning and reinforcement learning research. Rollback uses a lightweight LoRA pipeline to correct the world model's dynamics with real transitions from the policy it trains, a process the authors call test-time physics grounding. The system unifies distributed world-model search with asynchronous real-robot execution, and despite initialization from teleoperated demonstrations far below human level, it surpassed average human success rates on ball tossing and tabletop curling within 8 hours of training.

**Background**: World models are learned neural network simulators that predict future states conditioned on actions, offering a scalable alternative to real-world interaction for training robot policies. By constructing an exact coupling matrix from a second-order expansion of the loss and using its Fiedler vector to define an effective geometry, the authors perform real-space RG via block-spin aggregation and extract scaling exponents that match empirical estimates within 1–10%. It is likely to interest researchers in AI theory and physics-informed ML, though it is a research contribution rather than an immediate industry application. The study focuses on modular addition with a two-layer network, using an ensemble of trained models to define an order parameter (squared weight norm) and fluctuation proxies for heat capacity and susceptibility, with training epoch and weight decay acting as thermal and field control coordinates. The spectral ordering from the Fiedler vector yields a monotonic spatial decay of coupling strength absent under random permutations, and linearizing the local RG map produces relevant scaling exponents and five derived critical exponents.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: Grokking refers to a phenomenon where deep neural networks first memorize training data and only later, after many more training steps, suddenly generalize to unseen data. The renormalization group is a mathematical tool from theoretical physics that systematically describes how a system changes when viewed at different scales, often used to study phase transitions. This paper applies RG ideas to neural network training by treating neurons as degrees of freedom on a lattice and coarse-graining them via block-spin aggregation.

Every truncated result became broken JSON, and field loss was highly biased: one field reached the model in only 4.7% of calls while another in the same results reached it 99.3% of the time. Controlled experiments replaying 864 real tool results show the cut's real cost appears first as extra work rather than wrong answers: 43% more tool calls, twice the computation, and yield falling from 0.61 to 0.31, while the agent still finds the right answer when an alternative path exists. A new arXiv paper (2610.37055) introduces pre-commit noninterference (PNI), showing that audit-based certification of LLM agents is only valid if the audit coin is kept secret from the agent before it commits to an action, and quantifies the resulting bias as (1-ε)D_A, where D_A is the total-variation distance between the agent's views under the two coin values. Researchers introduce MLE-World, a world model finetuned from Qwen3.5-4B that predicts a program's terminal output (error traces, training logs, and validation scores) from its code and data description without executing it, along with a confidence score. On 17 MLE-bench Lite tasks, MLE-World matches the real terminal output on 77.9% of held-out programs, versus 41.1% for much larger prompted models, and its guided test-time scaling policies achieve up to 22.1% higher observed mean performance with less real execution. This work addresses a subtle but critical LLM safety risk: fine-tuning on seemingly benign data can silently erode safety, and standard content filters miss such data. It outperforms LLM-as-a-judge and prior gradient-based filtering, and the authors release SafeTulu along with a Hugging Face Space for customized filtering (e.g., changing removal fraction or subsets); analysis of removed data points to tool-execution failures and narrative arithmetic as possible under-studied sources of safety degradation.

A new arXiv paper (2610.37588) introduces a formal definition of faithful latent world models as an equivariance condition between the environment's transition map and the learned latent dynamics, and proposes latent rollout consistency (LRC) as a metric for action-conditioned latent prediction. Strikingly, the authors find that none of the studied state-of-the-art latent world models faithfully model the environment's dynamics, despite achieving good task performance. It provides the community with a rigorous evaluation tool (LRC) that could reshape how latent world models are assessed and guide future architecture design toward more faithful dynamics. The paper defines faithfulness via an equivariance condition: the learned latent transition should commute with the environment's transition map under the encoder. LRC measures consistency of multi-step latent rollouts under actions, and the empirical finding is that state-of-the-art models can succeed at tasks without satisfying this condition, suggesting they exploit shortcuts rather than true dynamics.

The pipeline outputs an annotated and revised version of the paper, a report of changes, and Lean code where each declaration is linked to the statement it formalizes; the author's toolkit grows as more papers are formalized, and verified papers can be shared for reuse. It is available at github.com/Jiyuan-Tan/PaperFormalizer, with shared papers at paperformalizer.org.

A new arXiv paper (2511.17671v2) identifies cross-user poisoning (CUP), an attack where an adversary injects a message into a shared multi-user agent context that is later applied when the agent serves a benign user, causing unauthorized actions. The authors validate CUP on two deployed multi-user agents, Continua and ElizaOS, and introduce MURMUR, a framework for evaluating shared-context agents under concurrent multi-user interactions. The findings show that robust multi-user agents require explicit user/task scoping rather than generic input filtering or context compression. Across Slack, Workspace, and Airline domains, CUP achieves high attack success, persists across later interactions, and remains substantially more effective than matched prompt-injection attacks. Evaluated defenses show that context summarization alone is insufficient, while task clustering and provenance prompting substantially reduce non-adaptive propagation.

CalArena introduces a standardized benchmark for post-hoc calibration, covering nearly 2000 experiments across tabular and computer vision tasks, and provides unified implementations of dozens of calibration methods. It also proposes Post-Hoc Improvement (PHI) in proper scoring rules as a principled alternative to traditional calibration error estimators. This benchmark addresses the reproducibility and evaluation gap in post-hoc calibration by enabling fair comparison of methods at scale, which is crucial for practitioners relying on reliable probability estimates. The benchmark aggregates predictions from classical models, deep learning architectures, and foundation models, and evaluates binary, multiclass, and large-scale classification settings. ## [The Trinity: Recursive Self-Improvement Framework for Multimodal Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36077) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The Trinity introduces a recursive self-improvement framework that couples world generation with Harness evolution through three roles—Creator, Explorer, and Evolver—and reorganizes tasks into a hierarchical capability tree. It reports mean performance gains of 34 points across 28 training benchmarks and 26 points across 18 unseen benchmarks, including two real-world embodied tasks. This work shifts task organization from surface categories to shared underlying capability requirements, potentially enabling more efficient and generalizable agent training across heterogeneous modalities. If validated, it could reduce the cost of building verifiable environments and manual Harness iteration, impacting how multimodal agents are developed and scaled. The framework uses Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real to abstract common requirements into simplified, verifiable simulated worlds for capability learning, while evaluation on original tasks measures transfer. Explorer evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree with validated updates accumulating within a fixed topology, and a Capability-Aware Harness Router selects compatible module configurations using public task information.

**Background**: Multimodal agents are AI systems that perceive and act across modalities such as text, images, and embodied environments. Harness evolution refers to automatically revising an agent's external scaffold—tools, prompts, and control logic—based on task feedback, while Real2Sim2Real is a paradigm that transfers policies from real data to simulation and back to reality for robust learning. The Trinity builds on these concepts by organizing tasks into a capability tree rather than surface categories, aiming to share capability requirements across diverse tasks.

A new arXiv paper (2610.36116) argues that science's indispensable aim is durable, collective human understanding and proposes a two-part test—human understanding and human direction—to determine when a research task can be delegated to AI. ## [StruPO: Structure-Aware Prompt Editor Preserves Scene Fidelity in Text-to-Image Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36146) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose StruPO, a structure-aware prompt editor that uses a calibrated scene graph as a shared representation for policy conditioning and image-grounded supervision, turning structural feedback into a training signal for a reusable editing policy. Experiments across three 2K-prompt test sets and four frozen generation backbones show consistent gains in relational fidelity and an improved faithfulness–aesthetics trade-off. This addresses a real problem in text-to-image generation: stylistic prompt rewriting often weakens object attributes and relations even when global text–image similarity remains high. A reusable one-pass editing policy could make prompt optimization more reliable and efficient, benefiting users who rely on precise scene control. StruPO handles uncertain grounding and stochastic image generation by retaining grounding confidence through smooth reward shaping and averaging multiple images per edit before computing group-relative advantages. The resulting policy produces optimized text in one pass after graph calibration, eliminating the iterative critique–rewrite loop, and human preference margins increase with relation complexity.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: Text-to-image models like diffusion models generate images from text prompts, but users often rewrite prompts stylistically to improve results, which can inadvertently drop or alter key attributes and spatial relations. Scene graphs represent objects, attributes, and relationships in a structured way, and reinforcement learning (specifically group-relative policy optimization) can train policies from reward signals. StruPO combines these ideas to learn a prompt editing policy that preserves the requested scene structure.

## [MARQ: Modular LLM-Agnostic Requirement Quality Assessor with Systems Engineering Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36234) ⭐️ 7.0/10

MARQ is a modular, LLM-agnostic prototype that infuses INCOSE systems engineering knowledge into LLMs to improve automated requirement quality assessment. On an expert-labeled NASA dataset, it achieved median F1 scores of 0.80 for Claude Opus 5, 0.62 for GPT-5.6 Sol, and 0.53 for Gemma 3 12B, compared to off-the-shelf baselines of 0.55, 0.52, and 0.18, respectively. This work shows that injecting domain-specific systems engineering knowledge can significantly boost LLM performance on requirements engineering tasks, even for smaller open-weight models, offering a model-agnostic pathway to more trustworthy AI-assisted requirements review. It matters for systems and requirements engineers who need reliable automated defect detection, and suggests that knowledge infusion can help close the gap between proprietary and open models. The gains are model-dependent: Claude Opus 5 improved both defect detection and false-alarm control, GPT-5.6 Sol gained detection and consistency at the cost of more false alarms, and Gemma 3 12B reached the performance of off-the-shelf proprietary models but remained highly variable. Criterion-level analysis shows improvements concentrated in Correctness and Conformance, with trade-offs between misses and false alarms within individual criteria, underscoring the need for criterion-specific interventions and human-in-the-loop review.

## [BehaveRec: Gated Three-Signal Framework for Sequential Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36239) ⭐️ 7.0/10

BehaveRec proposes a gated three-signal framework combining a causal session transformer, a bidirectional 90-day User History Encoder, and a GraphSAGE module over a user-user behavioral similarity graph. On an industrial dataset of 137M sequences from 12.6M users, it improves R@5 by +3.2% over SASRec, with the gain growing monotonically with history length and becoming negligible below ~10 interactions. This work moves beyond assuming that long-term history and community signals always help, providing a dose-response analysis and a practical deployment rule (~20 interactions per user) for when added complexity pays off. It offers industrial practitioners a principled way to decide when to invest in history and graph-based signals rather than session-only models. The advantage persists against a larger-capacity SASRec baseline (+2.5% R@5) with more parameters than BehaveRec, ruling out model capacity as the explanation. BehaveRec remains lightweight at 5.67M parameters and trains on a single GPU in under two days; however, the headline results are for category-level intent prediction, and a preliminary single-run check on full item-level vocabulary yields directionally mixed results, scoped as an open question.

## [RefactorProof benchmark reveals LLM-generated Lean proofs break under semantics-preserving refactoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36328) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced RefactorProof, a benchmark that derives 458 Lean-certified variants from 185 VERINA tasks by applying behavior-preserving refactorings while keeping the specification and evaluated proof byte-for-byte fixed. They found that task-normalized structural proof survival rate (PSR) is only 4.3% for VERINA's reference proofs and 13.3–26.8% for specialized provers, though on matched tasks specialized prover proofs (e.g., DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B, Goedel-Prover-V2-32B/8B) survive unchanged 15.6–20.3 percentage points more often than reference proofs. This work shows that LLM-generated formal proofs are often brittle: a proof that verifies against one implementation may fail after a semantics-preserving refactoring, which undermines the reliability of verifiable code generation pipelines. It provides a quantitative stress test that could push the community to evaluate proof stability, not just one-shot verification success, and to design provers that produce more refactoring-robust proofs. The benchmark holds specifications and proofs fixed byte-for-byte while applying structural refactorings, and the primary model-versus-reference comparisons are restricted to 21–25 short, non-recursive tasks because VERINA supplies reference proofs for only 46 tasks (all from its basic split). The authors caution that unchanged-proof failure is not the same as high repair cost: predefined one-identifier edits repair 51/54 eligible reference structural failures and 58/85 eligible prover failures, so RefactorProof measures stability, not maintenance cost.

**Background**: Lean is a proof assistant and functional programming language based on dependent type theory, widely used for formal verification and theorem proving. Refactoring means restructuring code without changing its behavior, so a proof that depends on the original code's structure may no longer apply even though the program's semantics are unchanged.

WAKMan introduces a workload-aware KV cache manager that dynamically selects an eviction policy based on live traffic, without needing to know request types or inspect prompts. Across 20 workload mixes, it improves cache hit rate over vLLM's default LRU by 5 percentage points on average and achieves the lowest mean and worst-case optimality gap among all policies. This work shows that no single eviction policy—including LRU or S3FIFO—is universally best for LLM serving, and that adaptive selection can deliver consistent gains across diverse traffic patterns. It is directly relevant to LLM infrastructure practitioners seeking to reduce prefill latency and serving costs in production systems. The paper finds that agentic steps return within seconds and favor recency, while popular prompts and long conversations favor frequency; LRU beats S3FIFO by 12% on agentic-heavy mixes but trails it by up to 22% elsewhere, and even a single workload parameter can flip the winner. WAKMan selects policies from live traffic without knowing request types or reading prompts, achieving the lowest mean and worst-case optimality gap.

A new empirical study introduces ReInBench, a dataset of 1,259 agent traces and 1,403 error events from computer-use and web tasks, analyzing how often and how quickly LLM agents self-recover from errors. ## [ATEMPO: Amortized Transfer Entropy Estimator Over Lags and Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36536) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ATEMPO introduces a diffusion-based transfer entropy estimator that is amortized over lags and time, allowing a single score network to estimate the full TE surface without refitting. It achieves the lowest mean relative error on synthetic datasets and 0.98±0.04 lag-detection accuracy, requiring only one fit for a 6×3 grid where existing estimators need 18 separate fits. This work significantly reduces the computational cost of transfer entropy estimation across multiple lags and time-varying delays, making it practical for large-scale time-series causal analysis. The recovered delays improve downstream forecasting, reducing MSE by 7.25% on WEATHER-5K and improving mean R² by 4.1% on brain-computer interface tasks. ATEMPO conditions explicitly on temporal position and samples source and conditioning depths during training, enabling estimation of the full TE surface. It is the only estimator to maintain perfect lag-detection accuracy across all evaluated window lengths on three systems with time-varying lag, and 120 selected inputs outperform the benchmark's 240-feature default by 4.6%.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: Transfer entropy is an information-theoretic measure of directed information flow between time series, defined as the reduction in uncertainty about a target's future given a source's past beyond the target's own history. Traditional estimators require separate fits for each combination of source and conditioning depths, and further estimation on local windows to track delays over time, which is computationally expensive. Diffusion models are generative models that learn to reverse a noise process, often using a score network, and have been adapted for amortized inference tasks.

A new arXiv paper introduces a decision-value framework showing that a monitor with fixed 90% accuracy can swing from a 5-point loss to a 35-point gain in agent success rate, depending solely on the replacement attempt's residual-budget success probability. This work challenges the common practice of evaluating AI agent restart monitors by classification accuracy alone, which can be misleading because the value of a restart depends on the probability that a new attempt succeeds with the remaining budget. In a study of 194 externally evaluated model executions on 19 SymPy issues from SWE-bench Verified, with a retrospective audit of 130 traces, the authors found a 2.29-point apparent restart gain traced to a single surviving failed attempt, a 42.29-point loss on a second model, no positive replication on prospective task cohorts, and zero of 103 live comparisons meeting the certification bar. The audit requires no additional model calls and returns 'abstain' when evidence is insufficient.

## [CASEL: Consequence-Aware Runtime Policy for Safer Tool-Using LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36570) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces CASEL (Consequence-Aware Selective Execution Layer), a model-agnostic runtime policy that chooses among direct execution, verification, sandboxing, clarification, approval, and abstention for each proposed tool call by minimizing a per-mode cost that combines calibrated failure probability, state-dependent consequence, reversibility, ambiguity, and evidence freshness. In a controlled simulation over 20 seeds with 120,000 test actions each, CASEL cut harmful-side-effect trajectories from 14.75% (uncertainty-ranked gate) to 7.02% and mean normalized harm from 0.184 to 0.123. As LLM agents increasingly modify external systems, runtime safeguards that allocate scrutiny by generic uncertainty scores or coarse mutation heuristics may be insufficient; CASEL's consequence-aware allocation offers a more principled way to reduce harmful side effects while managing human-approval load. The work is relevant to agent reliability and AI safety research, though its effectiveness is demonstrated only in simulation. A gate ranked by the product of failure probability and consequence achieved similar harm (5.82%, 0.120) but sent 45% more actions to human approval, while removing reversibility-aware routing raised the harm rate to 15.53%, and a trajectory-level risk budget increased harm at equal cost (11.82%). The authors explicitly note that intervention effectiveness is assumed rather than measured, so the results rank allocation rules under the simulator's assumptions and do not establish deployment effectiveness.

## [RuHarness co-evolves rubrics and harnesses for continual agent self-improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36826) ⭐️ 7.0/10

RuHarness proposes a rubric-harness co-evolution framework that continually discovers and reassesses behavioral criteria from execution trajectories, prioritizes unresolved weaknesses, and uses them to guide targeted harness updates while keeping the task objective fixed. Experiments across diverse agent tasks and backbone models show it outperforms strong harness-evolution baselines, especially on unseen held-out tasks. This addresses a key limitation in LLM agent evolution: static supervision that fails to track changing behavioral weaknesses across rounds, potentially limiting generalization. By dynamically adapting evaluation criteria, RuHarness enables more sustained self-improvement and stable generalization, which could benefit any system relying on autonomous agents for complex, open-ended tasks. The framework keeps the task objective fixed while co-evolving rubrics and harnesses, and its adaptive rubric prioritization is shown to track shifting weaknesses and support more stable generalization across evolution rounds. However, as an arXiv preprint, it lacks peer review and community discussion, and the abstract does not specify the exact benchmarks or model versions used.

**Background**: An agent harness is the engineered execution layer around an LLM that supplies context, memory, constraints, orchestration, tooling, and feedback to turn model intelligence into reliable, goal-directed behavior. Recent work has begun to evolve these harnesses from execution experience, but the supervision guiding evolution often remains static. Rubric-based evaluation uses explicit criteria to assess open-ended agent outputs, and continual learning aims to improve agents over time without forgetting. RuHarness combines these ideas by co-evolving rubrics and harnesses.

## [Approximate Policy Iteration for Zero-Sum Partially Observable Stochastic Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36847) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces an approximate policy-iteration algorithm for finite-horizon zero-sum partially observable stochastic games (zs-POSGs) that maintains one policy per player and updates both jointly along occupancy trajectories using conservative policy updates and a single supporting hyperplane per update. This approach avoids approximating a full central value function over high-dimensional occupancy spaces, potentially improving the runtime-exploitability trade-off at larger horizons compared to PBVI, HSVI, and CFR+, which could benefit multi-agent reinforcement learning and game theory research. The algorithm alternates local policy improvements, conservative updates, and persistent exploration, concentrating computation on occupancy regions where the current joint policy is exploitable; it is competitive at small horizons and often improves the runtime-exploitability trade-off at larger horizons on finite-horizon zero-sum POSG benchmarks.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: Partially observable stochastic games (POSGs) model multi-agent interactions under uncertainty where each agent has limited visibility of the true state. Zero-sum POSGs (zs-POSGs) are a subclass with opposing rewards. Occupancy-state reductions transform zs-POSGs into occupancy Markov games, enabling dynamic programming, but existing point-based solvers like PBVI and HSVI optimize a central value function and require point-based updates over high-dimensional occupancy spaces.

## [GUI-JEPA: Decoder-Free Latent Policy for Mobile GUI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36877) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose GUI-JEPA, the first decoder-free GUI agent policy built on a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), which scores candidate actions in a pretrained latent space in a single batched pass instead of decoding action tokens one by one. On AndroidControl it runs 2.8–4.0x faster than a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-7B agent on the same GPU while reaching 86–92% of that model's in-distribution accuracy with only 6% of its parameters. Mobile GUI agents are usually 7B-scale vision-language models whose token-by-token decoding makes them slow and memory-hungry, a real bottleneck for on-device deployment. GUI-JEPA shows that action selection can be moved into a compact latent space, potentially enabling much cheaper and faster agents without a large language model in the loop. The action- and region-conditioned latent predictor turns the screen latent into one latent per candidate action, and lightweight heads score all candidates against the instruction without decoding any token; notably, a randomly initialized predictor performs as well as one pretrained on screen dynamics, suggesting the predictor is trained for the decision itself. The work is an early arXiv preprint (2610.36877) with code released on GitHub.

Researchers introduce Dwell, a model-based reinforcement learning framework that reframes a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) as a recurrent latent transition operator, enabling the agent to predict, adjust, and act in latent space. Across five interactive visual environments, Dwell achieves the strongest overall performance among trainable methods while substantially reducing the compute required for imagination. This work shows that pretrained VLMs can be leveraged for efficient continual learning through online interaction without expensive full-model updates, potentially enabling agents that continually expand their capabilities. It also suggests that effective world models for VLM agents need not reconstruct the future, but only predict futures useful for action, which could lower the barrier to deploying model-based RL with large pretrained models. Dwell leverages the VLM's own representations and its dual role as both world model and policy, learning from real interactions to anticipate and evaluate action outcomes and from latent imagination to improve behavior. ## [AI uncovers better CNOT decomposition for remote transpositions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37045) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Using AlphaCNOT as an exploratory tool, researchers discovered a recurring CNOT decomposition for remote transpositions on constrained qubit topologies that requires at most 6d-4 CNOT gates, improving on the 6d-3 gates needed by SWAP-based routing. They formalized this into a deterministic synthesis method called Global Transpositions and identified a new mechanism called intermediate CNOT fusion. This work shows that AI-assisted synthesis can go beyond circuit optimization to uncover reusable identities and provable constructions, potentially guiding the design of new deterministic compilation algorithms for near-term quantum devices with limited connectivity. It offers certified upper bounds on CNOT cost and subsumes optimal SWAP routing, which could reduce overhead in quantum compilation. The discovered pattern yields a topology-legal implementation for two qubits at graph distance d>1 using at most 6d-4 CNOT gates, compared to 6d-3 for SWAP-based construction. The Global Transpositions method searches for a minimum-cost decomposition of an entire permutation into topology-aware logical transpositions, and intermediate CNOT fusion exploits temporary linear transformations that leave the permutation subgroup.

**Background**: Quantum computers have limited qubit connectivity, so logical operations between distant qubits must be decomposed into sequences of CNOT gates, often via SWAP routing that moves qubit states closer. AlphaCNOT is a reinforcement learning algorithm that minimizes CNOT gates in linear reversible circuits. This paper uses it to discover general principles for deterministic compilation rather than just optimizing individual circuits.

## [Correctness Filtering Biases Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37070) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.37070) formalizes how restricting chain-of-thought faithfulness evaluation to correctly answered instances introduces a selection bias, deriving the exact gap Δ = Cov(A, C)/P(C=1) via a seven-variable structural causal model. The authors confirm this empirically across four sub-ceiling deployments on arithmetic tasks, with a primary GLM-5.3 run showing a +7.4 percentage-point gap (n=1000, p<0.0001) and a pooled Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio of 1.70 (p<10^-6). This work reveals that a common evaluation practice—only measuring faithfulness on correct answers—can systematically distort conclusions about model interpretability, affecting how researchers compare CoT faithfulness across models and benchmarks. It provides a rigorous statistical framework and a protocol review of 18 papers, urging the interpretability community to account for selection effects or avoid correctness filtering when possible. The model distinguishes difficulty confounding from shortcut-induced collider bias and states the conditional-independence assumption needed to express the gap through latent response propensities. An assumption-free covariance decomposition attributes 42.8% of the GLM-5.3 gap to between-stratum variation in interventionable-operation count, leaving the majority unattributed; the paper notes that when counterfactual compliance is observable for every instance, evaluating all traces directly estimates population faithfulness without correctness filtering.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: Chain-of-thought (CoT) faithfulness evaluation measures whether a model's stated reasoning actually reflects the process behind its answer, rather than being post-hoc rationalization. In causal inference, collider bias occurs when conditioning on a common effect of two variables creates a spurious association between them; here, correctness can act as a collider when both faithfulness and difficulty influence whether an answer is correct. The Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test is a statistical method for assessing association between binary variables while controlling for stratification, commonly used in observational studies.

## [OpenGray benchmark evaluates LLM radiotherapy planning agents on decision quality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37081) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced OpenGray, a benchmark built on the OpenKBP-Opt head-and-neck dataset that adds tasks with known-correct planning decisions, including two dose-goal contradictions proven incompatible and a feasible control with a stored plan meeting all hard goals. They evaluated four systems, from a rule-based script to a full LLM agent using commercial Terra and local Ministral 3 8B models, on 30 patients, and also analyzed logs from 39 stereotactic radiosurgery runs of the clinical LLM agent SAGE. Current evaluation of radiotherapy planning agents relies mainly on achieved dose, which can mask specific decision failures; OpenGray shows that favorable aggregate scores can conceal critical errors such as failing to escalate contradictions or missing hard goals. This highlights the need to assess agent decisions explicitly and to provide actions for stopping and requesting review, which is important for safe clinical deployment of LLM-based agents in healthcare. With Terra, the script preceded by an LLM review and the full agent achieved decision accuracies of 95.4% and 92.1%, yet escalated only 50% and 25% of overlap contradictions that required arithmetic on the anatomy. All four systems submitted every feasible control, but 24% of these plans missed a hard goal that the stored plan had met, and in four SAGE runs one goal failed at every attempt while the agent identified it in every reply but had no action for stopping.

ReForest is a framework that converts Isolation Forest decision paths into natural-language explanations for LLM-based refinement, enabling uncertainty-aware dynamic ensemble of statistical and semantic anomaly signals. Experiments on four real-world datasets show an average 21% improvement in Recall and a 10% gain in F1-score over baselines. This hybrid approach addresses the semantic gap in statistical anomaly detection by combining efficiency with contextual reasoning, potentially improving high-stakes decision-making in domains like healthcare and finance. It also enhances model transparency by grounding semantic narratives in statistical evidence. The framework uses uncertainty-driven instance-level confidence to adaptively weigh statistical and semantic signals, and it provides interpretable rationales. However, the approach relies on LLMs, which can be expensive and slow, though the dynamic ensemble may mitigate this by selectively invoking the LLM.

**Background**: Isolation Forest is an efficient anomaly detection algorithm that identifies anomalies by isolating observations through random partitioning; anomalies are isolated faster because they are few and different. However, it lacks semantic understanding of the data context. Large Language Models (LLMs) have strong semantic reasoning abilities but are computationally intensive, making them impractical for large-scale anomaly detection alone. ReForest bridges this gap by using LLM reasoning to refine Isolation Forest results.

## [CauTrace: White-Box Framework Traces LLM Reasoning Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37369) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.37369) introduces CauTrace, a white-box diagnostic framework that characterizes ordinary and adversarially induced LLM reasoning failures using seven functional states, representation propagation across Transformer blocks, and temporal-state coordination. Evaluated on Qwen and LLaMA-family models, failed traces show weaker Attention-MLP agreement on support-state updates and less verification activity relative to commitment, with architecture-specific signatures. This work moves beyond endpoint correctness to reveal how failures develop internally, offering a unified diagnostic lens for AI safety and interpretability. It could help researchers and developers detect and mitigate reasoning failures in LLMs, especially under adversarial conditions. CauTrace defines seven functional states to represent support and constraint processing, measures how state changes persist across Transformer blocks, and analyzes when commitment and verification occur relative to support. Held-out repair and steering tests show consistent operational signals for certain models and settings, with aligned steering producing predicted directional changes in process measures.

## [Agent-Conditioned Routing Elicits Diverse Reasoning from Frozen MoE Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37375) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.37375) introduces Agent-Conditioned Routing (ACR), which assigns untrained shared/private expert-eligibility masks to parallel trajectories in a frozen sparse mixture-of-experts model while keeping the learned token router intact. On a screened 126-question math and physics benchmark, ACR roughly doubled the number of problems solved with at least two distinct primary methods compared to the strongest temperature sampling setting (37.3 vs 18.7 under GLM 5.3, and 45.00 vs 27.00 under GPT-5.6 Sol). It suggests a lightweight inference-time mechanism for exploiting the conditional capacity already present in sparse MoE architectures. ACR adds only about 160 KiB of mask state, and in a three-problem microbenchmark capped at 1,024 tokens its latency and peak VRAM usage stayed within 3% of batched temperature sampling. However, a blinded four-expert audit found more multi-method solutions with ACR but also lower correctness, and an informed sequential prompt that explicitly asks for alternative methods elicited even more diversity.

Researchers propose FoG, a framework that trains knowledge-graph (KG) agents to retrieve the supporting triples behind their answers using evidence-grounded synthesis, a KG interaction agent, and an evidence-coverage process reward (ECPR). Experiments on three KGQA benchmarks show that 3B–4B open-source agents trained with FoG outperform substantially larger baselines in both answer accuracy and evidence coverage, with zero-shot cross-KG transfer. By making evidence retrieval a first-class training objective, FoG could improve the trustworthiness and interpretability of retrieval-augmented agents in high-stakes domains. FoG's evidence-grounded synthesis recursively hides explicit entities behind verifiable sub-questions so that every question carries its supporting triples by construction, while ECPR credits each supporting triple to the turn that first retrieves it. The work is an early arXiv preprint (arXiv:2610.37405v1) and has not yet undergone peer review.

## [Concordat: Typed Sessions Enforce Safe LLM Agent Protocols](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37461) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Concordat is a new open-source Python library that models LLM agents as finite-state protocols using typestate and session types, enforcing legal tool calls and human-approval gates at runtime. In an evaluation on 50 airline tasks from tau-bench with simulated customers pressuring the agent to skip confirmation, the standard agent made unauthorized changes in 13 of 50 tasks with gpt-4.1 and in 29 of 128 task-runs with Claude Haiku 5.5, while the Concordat agent made none, with no significant difference in task success. This work addresses a critical safety gap in LLM agents that take consequential actions, such as cancellations or refunds, by providing a runtime enforcement mechanism that does not rely on the model's compliance with prompt instructions. It could influence how agent frameworks design safety guarantees and may lead to broader adoption of type-based protocol enforcement in production agent systems. Concordat checks protocols at definition time and rejects subclasses that could bypass their parent's protocol, a behavioral form of Liskov substitution. It also charges token and tool-call budgets linearly across handoffs, and notably, tau-bench's own reward did not detect most of the violations that Concordat prevented.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: Typestate programming encodes an object's runtime state into its compile-time type, ensuring that only valid state transitions are allowed. Session types ensure correctness in concurrent programs by guaranteeing that messages are sent and received in the expected order and type. Concordat applies these concepts to LLM agents, treating the agent's interface as a finite-state protocol so that only legal tool calls are offered at each turn, preventing unsafe actions before they have side effects.

## [CrossProfile Benchmark Exposes Memory Heuristic Failures in LLM Group Decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37624) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces CrossProfile, a diagnostic benchmark of 60 templates with automatically verified answer keys, crossing the ownership of supporting, decoy, and irrelevant facts while holding text fixed, yielding 480 tasks. Testing Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and two DeepSeek models shows that both rarest-first and relevance-based memory selection heuristics fail predictably, with relevance filters losing 23-31 points to rarest-first in hidden-profile settings. This work reveals systematic flaws in common memory compression strategies for LLM multi-agent systems, showing that accuracy depends on the balance of evidence kept rather than the selection policy. It has direct implications for designing reliable group decision-making pipelines and highlights the need for better memory management in collaborative LLM applications. The study finds that relevance-based selection readmits decoys because they are on-topic, and rarest-first selection is no better than random on average. Additionally, the decision model exhibits a social proof bias, giving extra weight to facts attributed to many agents; removing or randomizing attribution tags raises accuracy by 13-24 points in the classic configuration, and in natural discussions the complete transcript yields lower accuracy than no notes at all.

The paper introduces a temporal variability score (TVS), defined as the coefficient of variation of an item's negative log-likelihood across point-in-time models trained on web snapshots from different years. Evaluating six benchmarks with six models from multiple open-source families, the authors find that high-TVS items improve faster later in pretraining and outperform low-TVS items in 34 of 36 model-benchmark settings, with an average advantage of 7.3 points of chance-normalized accuracy. This work provides a diagnostic for understanding how different types of knowledge are acquired over the course of pretraining, moving beyond aggregate benchmark scores. It could help researchers design better data curricula and predict which knowledge items will benefit most from additional training. The TVS is computed as the coefficient of variation of an item's negative log-likelihood across point-in-time models, where a higher score indicates less consistent representation across years of web text. The pattern is most robust on knowledge-intensive tasks, even when comparing items of similar difficulty, and the analysis covers six benchmarks and six models from multiple open-source families.

## [KPPax converts KPP chemistry mechanisms into differentiable JAX code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37655) ⭐️ 7.0/10

KPPax is a kinetic preprocessor that translates chemical mechanisms written in the Kinetic PreProcessor (KPP) language into differentiable, just-in-time compiled, and vectorisable JAX code. It uses sparse operations in log space for rate laws and integrates stiff systems with diffrax's implicit solvers and forward/reverse-mode adjoints, enabling exact sensitivities without hand-derived adjoint code. This bridges atmospheric chemistry modeling with differentiable programming, allowing KPP mechanisms to be directly used for gradient-based parameter estimation and hybrid physics-machine-learning models. It could benefit scientific ML and chemistry modeling communities by enabling exact sensitivities and seamless integration with neural networks. On the POLLU benchmark, KPPax's Fisher information matrix predicted which of 25 rate coefficients a flow-tube-like design can identify, and noisy synthetic estimation confirmed uncertainties of nine identifiable coefficients to within about 30%, while revealing clusters of fast reactions where only ratios are constrained. A neural-network emission correction trained offline on 4D-Var retrievals and fine-tuned online reduced biogenic correction error by a factor of 2.4–5 and recovered low-temperature emission information.

ResCom introduces a low-rank correction that uses activation rounding residuals to compensate for layer-output errors in 4-bit weight-activation quantized LLMs, computed in closed form without gradient training. On Llama-3-8B, rank-32 attention corrections reduce WikiText-2 perplexity from 7.708 to 7.147, improve MMLU by 2.89 points, and raise five-shot GSM8K accuracy from 23.96% to 36.16%. This method significantly improves accuracy for low-bit weight-activation quantization without retraining, making efficient LLM deployment more viable for memory- and compute-constrained environments. It could enable broader adoption of 4-bit inference for large models from 1B to 70B parameters. The FP32 implementation adds 2.25% to 4K prefill time, while a separate compact-storage implementation retains a 27.7% peak-memory reduction relative to FP16. Evaluations extend to models from 1B to 70B parameters and held-out C4 data.

**Background**: Quantization reduces the memory and computation needed to deploy large language models by representing weights and activations with fewer bits. However, rounding activations to low-bit values introduces errors that calibration-based reconstruction cannot fully correct, because it cannot distinguish activations within the same quantization bin. ResCom addresses this by using the rounding residual to compute a low-rank correction that compensates for the resulting layer-output error.

The authors propose AgentBaton, a lightweight detector that learns when to hand off from task-progress patterns, reducing API costs by 65.9% on average across 11 model pairs and two benchmarks while largely preserving accuracy, with gains up to 8.8 percentage points. The study focuses on handoff direction and context transfer, finding that capable-to-efficient handoffs at suitable task-progress stages largely preserve or improve accuracy, while efficient-to-capable handoffs yield limited or no cost reduction. AgentBaton extends the empirical accuracy-cost Pareto frontier across various reasoning-effort settings, though as a preprint it lacks peer review and community discussion.

## [Layerwise Repacking Optimizes Variable-Length Hybrid-Attention Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35989) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Layerwise Repacking is a new technique that repacks samples from wide SP16/32 full-attention groups into node-local SP{1,2,4,8} sparse-attention children, eliminating an extra redistribution pass and cross-node all-to-all costs. On a 1F3S hybrid-attention model, it reduced mean end-to-end time by 5.95% and raised MFU by 3.75 percentage points; with an improved parent solver, time fell by 7.61% and MFU rose by 4.83 percentage points. This work addresses a real and non-obvious problem: reconciling conflicting parallelism requirements across full-attention and sparse-attention/MoE layers in variable-length training. The layerwise repacking approach, which avoids an extra redistribution pass by riding on existing communication, is a novel and practical optimization for large-scale distributed training of hybrid-attention models. The layout change rides on the two existing full-layer Ulysses sites: at each, one variable-size all-to-all performs both the head exchange and the sample repacking, so no redistribution pass is added. An auxiliary parent solver rebalances parent membership before the children are formed, because the balance the children can reach depends on which samples share a parent.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: Sequence parallelism (SP) splits the sequence dimension across multiple GPUs to handle long sequences, but different layers have different optimal SP degrees: full attention benefits from wide SP groups (e.g., 16 or 32) due to quadratic cost, while sparse-attention/MoE layers work well with smaller node-local groups (e.g., SP8). Switching between these groups changes which ranks own each sample, and a naive redistribution at every boundary would add costly data transfer. Hybrid-attention models combine full-attention and sparse-attention layers, and variable-length training further complicates load balancing.

A new arXiv paper (2610.35996) proposes approximating remote account states from transactions already recorded by both endpoint banks, enabling multi-layer GNN computation in federated anti-money laundering without additional account-specific data exchange. The study systematically tests a disclosure ladder that adds two transaction counts per remote account or the counterparty's own GNN states. Results show that counts provide a robust correction even under strong privacy protection, while exact remote states help only in specific regimes, and the noise needed to protect shared states erases their detection value before meaningful privacy is achieved.

## [UniTB: Universal E(3) Equivariant Hamiltonian Learning with DFTB Priors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36135) ⭐️ 7.0/10

UniTB introduces a universal E(3) equivariant Hamiltonian framework that integrates density-functional tight-binding (DFTB) physical priors with deep learning. Trained on 29,242 crystals, it achieves a 0.48 meV matrix-element error on nonmagnetic test crystals spanning 68 elements, and its UniTB-Flash variant assembles priors at O(N) cost using two-center tables. By generalizing across chemistries while keeping downstream properties physical, UniTB could enable efficient screening of disordered solids and new compositions for industrial applications. UniTB uses a mixture of experts routed by the DFTB prior and a charge-equilibration head as in self-consistent-charge tight binding, with a projection that bounds band shifts to suppress spurious states. The authors also provide the fastest SO(2) tensor-product GPU kernels for the network, and UniTB-Flash reduces prior assembly from O(N log N) on a grid to O(N) with two-center tables.

## [Axiomatic Framework Distinguishes Replication from Corroboration in Multi-Agent Debate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36151) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces root replication invariance (RRI) as a formal criterion for judges in multi-agent debates, proving it is equivalent to threshold-uniform replication immunity and that occurrence-sensitive and content-keyed judges admit profitable deviations. It also establishes an information boundary showing that no judge can both ignore replicas and respond strictly to fresh roots if its observation interface cannot distinguish them, and introduces the lineage quotient as the coarsest representation sufficient for replication-invariant judging. This work provides a theoretical foundation for designing debate judges that correctly weight independent evidence versus repeated reports, which is crucial for LLM evaluation and aggregation where agents may relay or paraphrase the same source. It could influence how multi-agent debate systems are built to avoid overcounting redundant information. The framework is lifted to quantitative bipolar argumentation frameworks (QBAFs), with strict fresh-root response characterized and its propagation along sign-consistent paths proven under DF-QuAD, yielding a tight closed-form response modulus. Exhaustive audits over 28,224 direct-star profiles, 2,052 multi-layer DAGs, and matched interventions on 277 AVeriTeC-derived profiles confirm the predicted separation between replication and corroboration under a supplied partition.

**Background**: Multi-agent debate is a technique where multiple LLM agents exchange arguments to reach a more accurate judgment, often used to improve factuality and reasoning. Distinguishing these is important for aggregating evidence correctly, but simple counting methods conflate them. This paper formalizes the problem using game theory and axiomatic design.

## [AI agent commits detectable without signatures, study finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36229) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A large-scale study of 7,837,946 commits from 1,226 repositories shows that AI coding agent commits can be distinguished from human commits even after authorship signatures are masked, achieving a ROC AUC of up to 0.859. Most of the signal comes from commit message verbosity and change size rather than code content. This finding is significant because prior empirical studies rely on optional signatures like bot accounts and Co-authored-by trailers, which may undercount agent activity. The results suggest signature-free detection can help prioritize commits for review but cannot replace recorded attribution, and that signature-based labels should be treated as a lower bound. On the full test set, the best detector reaches only 0.332 precision at the observed agent share, and detection transfers poorly to held-out Claude Code and Copilot, with TF-IDF achieving an AUC of just 0.524 for Claude Code. Temporal patterns also vary by agent, with Copilot's AUC dropping and later recovering, while more training history helps Claude Code but not Copilot.

## [Freeze Pretrained Policy to Improve No-Retention Offline-to-Online RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36247) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper identifies an actor-side failure in no-retention offline-to-online reinforcement learning: continued behavioral cloning (BC) refits the policy to limited, nonstationary online data, erasing the offline prior. It shows that freezing the pretrained expressive policy while continuing value learning substantially improves fine-tuning across IFQL, FQL, and QC on seven OGBench domains. This challenges the common assumption that offline data remains available during fine-tuning and offers a simple fix for settings where it does not, such as privacy or storage constraints. The insight could inform the design of more robust offline-to-online RL algorithms and prevent performance collapse when data retention is impossible. The failure is traced to a behavioral feedback loop: continued online BC rapidly erases the pretrained prior, causing representational collapse and loss of action diversity that starves the critic of exploration. Freezing the prior breaks this cycle, preserving offline coverage while allowing value learning to drive improvement; results are validated on seven OGBench domains across three methods.

## [AdvGuard: Graph-Based Detection of Multi-Turn System Prompt Leakage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36295) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers present AdvGuard, a model-agnostic framework that detects query-based system prompt leakage by modeling cross-query relationships with a bounded semantic interaction graph and classifying them using graph convolutional networks (GCNs). In multi-turn workloads it achieves 97.23%–99.1% F1 with 100% recall, and when integrated into the adaptive PLeak and LeakAgent attack loops it limits exact-match leakage to 0.00–0.01. Most existing defenses evaluate each query in isolation, so they miss malicious intent that only emerges across coordinated multi-turn interactions. AdvGuard's cross-query detection addresses this gap and is directly relevant to any organization deploying black-box LLM services that rely on proprietary system prompts for safety policies and access controls. AdvGuard statistically filters candidate components, converts the interaction graph into line graphs for GCN classification to capture multi-hop query-similarity patterns, and includes a lightweight prompt-level detector that protects before enough interaction history accumulates. In mixed-query evaluations it improves recall by up to 36% over the strongest baseline while keeping the false positive rate at or below 3.4%, and leave-one-attack-family-out tests show 99.98% mean recall with no observed false positives.

The paper introduces NextEval, an agent-based solver for derivative-free optimization (DFO) that integrates a large language model (LLM) to guide sequential selection of evaluation points under limited budgets. It also presents NextEval Bench, a benchmark protocol for comparing agent configurations on shared DFO tasks under matched evaluation budgets and information constraints. This work demonstrates a novel application of LLM agents to scientific optimization workflows, potentially improving evaluation efficiency in costly black-box settings. The accompanying benchmark enables fair comparison of agent configurations, which could accelerate research in LLM-guided optimization. The system combines an LLM agent with a numerical environment that provides tools for analyzing past evaluations and executing numerical methods, while maintaining a shared evaluation history and method-specific state to support continuation across method switches. Numerical results on low-dimensional DFO problems show that NextEval outperforms state-of-the-art DFO baselines in function-evaluation efficiency.

## [AutoProfiler learns kernel-conditioned profiling trees for LLM GPU optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36576) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose AutoProfiler, a feedback-driven framework that learns a deterministic, kernel-conditioned profiling tree from optimization feedback, iteratively refined via REWRITE and SPLIT operations with an LLM generating candidate modifications and empirical evaluation determining acceptance. Experiments on KernelBench show it improves kernel optimization over fixed profiling configurations under constrained profiling budgets. This work challenges the common assumption that collecting more profiling metrics is always better, showing that selective, kernel-specific profiling can outperform fixed strategies and suggesting profiling itself should become a reasoning dimension for LLM-driven GPU kernel optimization. The theoretical analysis shows that under heterogeneous profiling utility, kernel-conditioned selection can outperform any single fixed profiling configuration, and once the tree is built, the LLM rewriter is invoked only once per kernel, reducing overhead. The code is available on GitHub, but the work is an arXiv preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

## [Req2Test-Bench: LLM Agents Struggle with Behavioral Adequacy in Requirement-to-Test Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36584) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Req2Test-Bench, a benchmark of 5,086 execution-validated instances derived from developer-authored BDD artifacts across 8 open-source projects, 5 programming languages, and 4 BDD frameworks. Each instance pairs a Gherkin natural-language requirement with a developer-written test implementation, and evaluation of 8 agent-model-reasoning configurations shows that while the best configuration (Codex with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash) produces passing tests for 82.8% of instances, only 33.8% are behaviorally adequate. This benchmark addresses an understudied problem—black-box requirement-to-test generation—and reveals a substantial gap between execution success and behavioral adequacy, highlighting that current LLM agents may produce tests that pass but fail to validate the required behavior. The findings have implications for using LLM agents to generate validation harnesses that guide code generation from natural-language requirements. Behavioral adequacy is measured strictly as kill-completeness: a test is kill-complete if it kills every mutant that the ground-truth test kills. The study finds that scaling up agents yields sharply diminishing returns in behavioral adequacy relative to generation cost, and that under-specified requirements—including ambiguous setup and implicit expected outcomes—cause the information gap.

## [Balanced Truncation Compresses Mamba-2 States Along Write-Read Subspaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36617) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.36617) proposes a post-training balanced-truncation transform for Mamba-2 that compresses recurrent states along write-read subspaces rather than individual coordinates. The method, combined with a rank-allocation scheme called HARP, halves the state dimension with only a 0.3-point (1.8%) average WikiText-2 perplexity increase across models from 130M to 2.7B parameters, compared to a 1.6-point (9.3%) increase for GHOST. Mamba-2's fixed-size recurrent state dominates decoding memory and bandwidth, so more effective state compression directly reduces inference cost for state-space models. This work shows that classical control-theory balanced truncation, adapted to the model's structure, outperforms existing coordinate-wise quantization and pruning approaches, potentially making long-context SSM inference more practical. The key empirical finding is that state energy is nearly rank-one but concentrated in a bias-like direction accumulated by the recurrence, while output-relevant content lives in a low-dimensional subspace misaligned with the state's coordinates. The transform uses full controllability and observability Gramians and applies the rotation exactly via Mamba-2's scalar-identity transition; calibration requires only a single forward pass, an order of magnitude faster than GHOST's protocol with lower peak memory, and HARP allocates ranks per layer from the Hankel spectrum while protecting retrieval-sensitive layers.

Existing Mamba-2 state compressors quantize state values or prune state coordinates, scoring each channel independently in the native basis.

Dream-COP introduces a policy agent that learns executable policies by 'dreaming' in an experience world formed from past search trajectories and their outcomes, guiding a discovery agent to generate and refine combinatorial optimization programs. Tap2Listen introduces a streaming audio-visual target speaker extraction model that decouples audio and visual processing, allowing target switches with only a 0.12ms re-projection. The model separates computation by modality: a target-agnostic audio encoder processes only the mixture, while target-specific visual cues condition only the decoder. Component-wise losses are used—a prediction loss for the encoder and a supervised extraction loss for the decoder—and the system runs in real time on a single CPU core.

Researchers propose LOWN, a training-free decoding method for diffusion vision-language models (DVLMs) that decides at each denoising step whether to process the image. By comparing LLaDA-V's predictions with and without the image, they find that removing the image changes an unmasked token at only 22.8% of steps on average (as few as 7.9%), and LOWN exploits this by reusing image-free predictions when they agree with the last image-conditioned prediction, retaining 99.6% of LLaDA-V's score on ten benchmarks at 35.3% of the decoding FLOPs. LOWN requires no training or tuned threshold, generalizes across LLaDA-based DVLMs, and runs under key-value caching for further efficiency gains. The need for the image varies across benchmarks, which motivates an adaptive per-step decision rather than a fixed schedule; code and a project page are available.

A new arXiv paper applies collective predictive coding (CPC), a theory originally developed for language and symbol emergence, to classical spin systems, showing that macroscopic order parameters emerge automatically from atom-level predictive communication. The authors demonstrate this on 2D ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Ising models, a 2D model with competing stripe orders, and the fully connected Sherrington–Kirkpatrick spin-glass model, where the replica overlap emerges without reference to microscopic Hamiltonians. The approach relies only on observed spin configurations and does not require knowledge of the microscopic Hamiltonian or Lagrangian.

## [Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36794) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Select-TTT introduces a query-conditioned selective fast-weight update rule for In-Place Test-Time Training (TTT), scaling each chunk's write strength by its relevance to the user query. This relevance signal is derived without supervision or new parameters from the model's frozen output head, and a temperature-scaled softmax converts scores into learning-rate multipliers, consistently improving long-context QA on two benchmarks and two backbones. This work addresses a key limitation of In-Place TTT—its uniform write schedule that dilutes query-relevant information—with a simple, parameter-free rule, making TTT more practical for realistic long-context QA. It could benefit researchers in efficient LLM adaptation and long-context applications, and may extend to long-horizon agent tasks involving multiple user queries over evolving contexts. The relevance score is computed as the probability mass that a chunk's hidden states assign to the query tokens via the frozen output head, requiring no additional supervision or parameters. A temperature-scaled softmax turns these scores into learning-rate multipliers, preserving the chunk-wise, context-parallel computation of In-Place TTT; improvements are demonstrated on two benchmarks and two backbones.

**Background**: Test-time training (TTT) allows a deployed language model to internalize incoming context on-the-fly into a small set of fast-weight parameters, rather than treating it as transient attention context. In-Place TTT made this practical for large models by repurposing the down-projection of standard MLP blocks as fast weights, but its uniform write schedule causes irrelevant content to dilute query-relevant information in fast-weight memory, especially on realistic web long-context QA.

## [TAPESTRY: A Single Backbone for Video Generation and Robot Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36823) ⭐️ 7.0/10

TAPESTRY introduces a world action model that treats robot actions as single-patch tokens in a pretrained video diffusion transformer's latent space, enabling efficient robot policy learning without video generation at inference. It achieves 84 ms per action chunk on consumer hardware and outperforms comparable joint video-action policies in simulation and real-robot experiments. This approach significantly reduces inference cost for robot policies that leverage video generation models, making them more practical for real-time control. It also demonstrates a novel way to repurpose pretrained video backbones for embodied AI without retraining from scratch. The shared backbone is optimized with three diffusion objectives: video diffusion on VAE latents from robot and human videos, joint video+action diffusion with a coupled timestep and asymmetric attention mask, and action-only diffusion conditioned on clean image latents. At test time, actions are generated in a single DDIM step from pure noise, avoiding full video generation.
