## [PICO: Policy-Compatible Joint Decoding for Hard-Problem Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36849) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Policy-Compatible Reinforcement Learning (PICO), a method that overcomes the learning cliff in RLVR when all rollouts fail by generating expert trajectories that are both verifiably correct and compatible with the current policy. PICO performs distribution-constrained joint decoding, using expert data to guide token-level decoding while preserving the student's relative token probabilities, and a dynamic top-k mechanism confines sampling under a finite divergence budget. This work addresses a known limitation of RLVR—zero-advantage collapse on problems beyond the model's current ability—which can stall reasoning improvement on hard tasks. By providing a useful learning signal even when all on-policy rollouts fail, PICO could enable more effective reinforcement learning for complex reasoning and agentic benchmarks. PICO optimizes the generated trajectories jointly with on-policy rollouts under a mixed-behavior objective that uses importance sampling to mitigate distribution mismatch. Experiments across reasoning datasets and agentic benchmarks show that PICO consistently outperforms standard RLVR and prior off-policy baselines.

**Background**: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves LLM reasoning by using binary rewards from on-policy exploration, but group-relative estimators like GRPO and RLOO compute advantages relative to a group of rollouts. When every rollout fails, all rewards are identical, so the advantage collapses to zero and no learning signal remains—a phenomenon known as the learning cliff. Expert trajectories can provide supervision, but they often lie in low-probability regions of the student policy, causing large parameter shifts and surface-level imitation rather than transferable reasoning.

It suggests that agentic software assurance should prioritize deterministic evidence admission and careful feedback interpretation rather than simply adding more model contexts. On 160 OWASP Benchmark cases, model configurations trade clearance against unresolved outcomes, and the ten-context arm assesses only 96 cases; on two sets of 120 evidence packages, models reject 70-100% of applicable counterexamples, while construction-specific scope checks classify every package correctly. A new arXiv paper uses model stitching to show that the primary Lund plane representation is inherently weaker than the Particle Transformer (ParT) for jet tagging, and that this deficit is representational rather than computational. ## [FS-EWC: Fisher-Shaped EWC for Replay-Free Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37145) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose Fisher-Shaped EWC (FS-EWC), which reformulates Elastic Weight Consolidation to minimize the worst-case empirical Fisher information trace over a neighborhood of future parameter updates, rather than only protecting historically important parameters. At task completion, trajectory-based model merging constructs the retained solution from multiple optimization states before re-estimating the Fisher information matrix for subsequent consolidation. This work shifts the role of the Fisher information matrix from local parameter protection to solution formation for future retention, potentially improving the stability–plasticity balance in replay-free continual learning. If validated broadly, it could offer a principled alternative to replay-based methods for sequential learning without storing past data. FS-EWC explicitly favors solutions that are less sensitive to bounded future displacement by minimizing the worst-case empirical FIM trace within a prescribed neighborhood, and it uses trajectory-based model merging from multiple optimization states instead of a single terminal iterate. Experiments across multiple benchmarks show improved performance over standard EWC, with controlled studies indicating greater tolerance to parameter drift.

The paper proves that degree gating strictly outperforms any selection or reweighting of a relation when part of the population is isolated on that relation and the attacker cannot afford to open the gate, and that this window is sharp. The exposure bound extends to message passing and is computed without any attack; supporting tools give exact worst cases for linear relational models, certified brackets for R-GCN and tree ensembles, and a finite-sample guarantee for adversarial validation. Clean-trained graph detectors fall below their graph-free counterparts in 58 of 90 settings on six graphs, and the selection protocol mostly abstains with at most four relations, with cost-aware proposals helping only when relations are many (shown on synthetic graphs).

## [AdaRoll-GRPO: Bayes-Adaptive MDP for Rollout Allocation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37429) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces AdaRoll-GRPO, which reformulates rollout budget allocation in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) as a Bayes-adaptive Markov decision process (MDP) to learn an offline policy that allocates more rollouts to difficult questions and fewer to easy ones. Experiments on multiple reasoning datasets and LLM architectures show consistent training improvement under the same total rollout budget as standard GRPO. GRPO is widely used in LLM post-training for reasoning, but its uniform rollout budget wastes compute on easy questions and starves hard ones of informative reward signals. AdaRoll-GRPO offers a plug-in way to improve training utility without increasing the total rollout budget or adding online optimization overhead, which could make RL-based post-training more compute-efficient. The adaptive allocation policy is computed offline and applied during GRPO training, so no additional online optimization overhead is introduced. The method targets the same total rollout budget as standard GRPO, and the abstract reports gains across multiple reasoning datasets and LLM architectures, though specific quantitative results are not given in the abstract.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is a reinforcement learning algorithm for LLM post-training that removes PPO's separate value model and estimates each response's advantage by comparing its reward to the average reward of a group of responses sampled for the same prompt. Standard GRPO samples a fixed number of rollouts per question, regardless of difficulty. A Bayes-adaptive Markov decision process (BAMDP) is a framework for sequential decision-making under model uncertainty, where the agent maintains a belief over unknown model parameters and updates it via Bayes' rule as it acts.

## [FeatureArc Benchmark Tests Coding Agents on Evolving Features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37434) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced FeatureArc, a new benchmark that evaluates coding agents on their ability to handle evolving software features by constructing multi-stage tasks from repository histories. The benchmark was used to evaluate 10 coding agents on 73 manually reviewed tasks spanning 2 to 10 stages across four programming languages, revealing a drop in success from 62.7% at the first stage to 28.5% for the whole feature. Most existing benchmarks evaluate coding agents on a single request against a fixed codebase, but real-world development involves successive extensions built on earlier code. FeatureArc addresses this gap by measuring whether agents can maintain correctness across evolving features, an important capability for autonomous software engineering. The pipeline validates fail-to-pass (F2P) tests for new behavior and pass-to-pass (P2P) tests for existing behavior on reference code before and after each stage. Each agent works in one persistent session and workspace without external test feedback or rollback, and trajectory analysis found inherited defects in 72.9% of failed later stages, with agents leaving earlier errors unnoticed about 95% of the time.

**Background**: Coding agents are AI systems that can autonomously write, modify, and test code. Benchmarks like SWE-bench evaluate them on resolving issues in real repositories, but typically as isolated single-request tasks. FeatureArc builds on this by using repository histories to create tasks where a feature is extended over multiple stages, testing whether agents can build on their own earlier code without human intervention.

GEARS adaptively selects representations at test time, demonstrating that reasoning about unseen states requires more than generating RGB views.

## [200 LLM Trading Agents Herd When They Communicate, Study Finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37448) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.37448) ran 200 LLM agents from four model families in groups of ten under five communication regimes—from full isolation to message boards and shared notes—over seven US trading days (October 1–9, 2026). In two of the four families, communicating groups held far more of the same stocks than isolated groups, and a group's return was largely explained by the return on its members' common holdings. This is one of the first controlled empirical studies showing that communication among independent LLM trading agents can produce convergence and herding rather than better collective decisions, which matters for anyone deploying multi-agent LLM systems in financial markets. It also suggests regulators and researchers must measure excess convergence against a no-peer baseline, since even isolated agents converged on the same stocks. Seeing a groupmate's post made an agent 7 percentage points more likely to reuse an eight-word phrase from it, and agents that were too far apart to see each other's posts still shared such a phrase in 14% of cases—the rate attributable to common inputs. Notably, seeing the post did not detectably change that morning's trades, and communicating groups sold in step more often than isolated ones.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: Large language models (LLMs) are neural networks trained on vast text corpora, and recent work has begun using them as autonomous agents that can make decisions in simulated environments. Most prior multi-agent communication research assumes a shared objective with fast, clear feedback, but trading is different: each agent manages its own account and is scored late and noisily by markets, making a trading swarm a population of independent decision-makers where convergence is a risk rather than a goal. Herding—where investors crowd into the same positions—is a well-known source of systemic risk in financial markets, and central banks such as the Bank of England have begun stress-testing AI agents for it.

## [PerceptRL: Rule-Based RL Turns Caption Errors into Perception Training for MLLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37471) ⭐️ 7.0/10

PerceptRL introduces a reinforcement learning post-training method that uses a multi-agent pipeline to extract verified errors from dense image captions and convert them into QA pairs with fixed answer labels and rule-based rewards. It combines single-turn Perception RL, multi-turn Perception Agentic RL with visual tools, and a Coordinate Injection technique to correct spatial operations, achieving 71.6% average accuracy across seven benchmarks. Fine-grained visual perception is a known bottleneck in MLLM post-training, and PerceptRL shows that verifiable rule-based rewards can be derived from caption errors to strengthen perception without subjective reward models. Its 15.7-point gain over the base model with the same tools and 5.2-point lead over the strongest evaluated frontier VLM suggest a practical path for improving multimodal post-training. The method links correlated errors via Chain QA and combines unrelated errors in multiple-choice QA, with a specialized route for high-error domains and a domain-agnostic general route. It also addresses coordinate drift in tool-using models through Coordinate Injection in cold-start trajectories and a grounding-aware process reward that supervises intermediate spatial fidelity alongside final-answer correctness.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) process images and text together, and their post-training often focuses on reasoning while assuming perception is already adequate. Dense image captioning provides rich visual descriptions that can be used for pre-training, but continuing caption supervision during post-training is hard because captions are subjective and information-dense, making reward design difficult. Reinforcement learning with rule-based rewards offers a verifiable alternative to learned reward models, and PerceptRL applies this idea to perception by converting caption errors into QA tasks with fixed answers.

## [First Strategyproof Deep RL Mechanism for Online Resource Allocation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37504) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced the first strategyproof deep reinforcement learning mechanism for online resource allocation, using a monotonic neural network that guarantees truthful reporting by construction. The approach combines a generalized critical payment rule with training via RL or imitation, achieving 97.8% of an offline welfare upper bound on a four-resource stream. This work bridges mechanism design and deep RL, enabling more expressive allocation rules while preserving strong incentive guarantees, which could improve efficiency in online markets and resource allocation systems where strategic behavior is a concern. The monotonic neural network ensures that higher reported value cannot reduce acceptance, while longer duration or larger resource requirements cannot increase it; the critical payment is the lowest accepted value with other inputs fixed. Imitation learning reaches 97.5% of the upper bound in 261 seconds, about 89 times faster than RL training.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: Strategyproofness is a property of mechanisms where agents cannot benefit from misreporting their private information, ensuring truthful behavior. Online resource allocation involves assigning scarce resources to arriving tasks without knowing future demand, and reinforcement learning can adapt policies but typically lacks incentive guarantees. Monotonic neural networks are designed to preserve monotonic relationships between inputs and outputs, which is key to enforcing strategyproofness by construction.

The paper introduces parameterized steering, which sets activations to a desired trait strength rather than pushing them in a direction, and rescales the steering range to the most steerable interval for each vector. It also proposes orthogonalizing steering vectors to decouple multiple traits, enabling simultaneous control without interference. This work addresses two key challenges in activation steering: consistent steering strength with interpretable magnitude, and interference between multiple steering vectors. It could enable more reliable and fine-grained inference-time control of LLM behavior for researchers and practitioners. The method identifies the most steerable interval per steering vector and rescales the steering range accordingly, and orthogonalization decouples traits so that exhibiting one behavior does not induce others. ## [Paper formalizes 'structure gap' challenging the scaling hypothesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37523) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.37523) introduces the 'structure gap' to formalize the finite-data limitations of structure-agnostic learning compared to methods that incorporate explicit domain knowledge. The paper proves that for structure-encoded problems, a structured solver can achieve Bayes risk while a dense empirical learner has persistent excess risk, and it provides a cell-coverage lower bound and an unobserved-orbit non-identifiability result. This work challenges the prevailing scaling hypothesis in AI by arguing that more data cannot always replace structured reasoning, which could influence how researchers design models and incorporate domain knowledge. It has implications for machine learning theory and practice, especially in domains where data is limited or structure is known. The paper proves the structure gap exactly for a Gaussian inverse problem: the known-operator Wiener solver attains Bayes risk, while the dense empirical learner in the correct linear class has persistent expected excess risk. It also includes controlled experiments in known-operator inversion, sparse recovery, and graph reachability with size extrapolation to instantiate the mechanisms.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: The scaling hypothesis in AI posits that sufficiently large models trained on sufficiently large datasets can learn any pattern without explicit domain knowledge. Structure-encoded problems are tasks whose input-output mapping is determined or constrained by known structures like physical laws, grammars, or optimization objectives. The paper argues that while neural networks may be expressive enough to represent the desired mapping, finite data leaves residual uncertainty that structure can resolve by construction.

## [Uncertainty quantification fails under clinical class imbalance, new framework proposed](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37561) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper demonstrates that standard uncertainty quantification in selective prediction becomes a proxy for class membership under severe clinical class imbalance, systematically penalizing minority patients. The authors propose a framework combining class-conditional risk (CCR) with threshold-aware metrics that restores strict monotonicity and maintains balanced risk across 56 synthetic conditions and three real neurodegenerative cohorts (multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease). This work exposes a safety-critical flaw in clinical AI pipelines that rely on selective prediction, showing that a widely trusted safety mechanism can silently exclude the most vulnerable patients. It offers a practical correction, urging practitioners to adopt threshold-aligned uncertainty measures and class-stratified evaluation to ensure equitable deployment. The paper shows that applying CCR with standard entropy fails to protect the minority because it breaks within-class monotonicity when tau=0.5, whereas combining CCR with threshold-aware metrics restores strict monotonicity and correctly identifies ambiguous patients. Experiments span severe class imbalance to near-balanced conditions, and global metrics either collapsed minority sensitivity or protected the minority at the expense of majority patients.

**Background**: Selective prediction, also known as prediction with a reject option, allows a model to abstain on ambiguous cases and defer them to human experts, improving safety in high-stakes settings like clinical AI. This safety guarantee depends on uncertainty scores accurately reflecting clinical ambiguity, but in prognostic tasks where the outcome of interest is a minority class, standard uncertainty measures may instead capture class sparsity. The paper investigates this failure mode and proposes corrections to maintain balanced risk across patient groups.

## [MuonGS: Relaxed Weight-Norm Control for LLM Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37647) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces MuonGS, a variant of the Muon optimizer that uses Gram-Schmidt projection to remove the radial component of each update, guaranteeing that the accumulated effective learning rate grows as Ω(√T) and the weight norm grows at most proportionally to √t. In pretraining experiments with 160M- and 400M-parameter dense models and a 135M active/1B total MoE model, MuonGS achieves lower validation perplexity than MuonH at long horizons, with up to ~15% token-equivalent speedup for dense models. This work provides a unified theoretical explanation for why weight-norm control helps in Muon and shows that less restrictive norm control can sustain effective learning later in training, potentially leading to more efficient LLM pretraining. It offers a principled alternative to hard norm constraints like MuonW and MuonH. The analysis uses the accumulated effective learning rate C_T = Σ η_t/||W_t||_F and proves that vanilla Muon accumulates only logarithmically, while MuonGS guarantees C_T = Ω(√T) and an O(T^{-1/2}) stationarity guarantee for smooth scale-invariant objectives. The speedup estimate is based on matched validation loss and is specific to the tested model sizes and training horizons.

Judea Pearl and co-authors introduce epsilon-identifiability, a method that allows approximate identification of causal effects and counterfactual probabilities when exact identification from available data is impossible. This work provides a principled way to extract useful causal information even when exact identification is unattainable, broadening the scope of causal inference in fields where data are limited. The method caches each anchor pair's trajectories once, so subsequent student training does not require serving multiple live anchor models concurrently, which keeps the pipeline practical. ## [AOS-Bench: New Benchmark Tests LLM Agents as Workload Managers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33178) ⭐️ 7.0/10

AOS-Bench is a new benchmark that evaluates LLM coding agents as workload managers handling streams of tasks under shared CPU and memory limits, revealing that isolated task success does not carry over to dynamic workloads. Across five model-harness pairs, heavy workloads cause every system to lose 13 to 23 points, and two systems 0.6 points apart in isolation deliver 54% and 68% of the same tasks. This work identifies workload management as a distinct capability for agents, separate from isolated task-solving ability, which could reshape how agent systems are designed and evaluated. It matters for developers building persistent coding assistants that must juggle multiple pending jobs on one machine. Execution-policy interventions trace much of the gap to task intake: serial dispatch leaves 73% of heavy-workload tasks unclaimed, yet a fixed concurrency of two comes within four points of the best agent-managed policy. Under every policy, median CPU use stays below 30% of provisioned cores while tasks wait, suggesting more elaborate management does not necessarily help.

**Background**: LLM coding agents are increasingly used as persistent assistants that receive a stream of work—such as builds, data-processing jobs, and bug fixes—rather than one request at a time. Existing benchmarks evaluate each task in isolation, so they cannot measure how well an agent schedules, overlaps, and delegates tasks under shared CPU and memory constraints. AOS-Bench fills this gap by having verified tasks arrive over time and requiring delivery under shared resource limits, with the same tasks run one at a time as a per-system reference.

## [SkipCat: Rank-Maximized Low-Rank Compression for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13494) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SkipCat introduces a low-rank compression framework that combines intra-layer shared low-rank projection and block skipping to retain higher ranks under the same compression budget, achieving a 7% accuracy improvement on zero-shot tasks without fine-tuning compared to previous methods. This work addresses the trade-off between compression rate and performance in low-rank compression, offering a practical solution for deploying large language models on resource-constrained edge devices without significant accuracy loss. The method uses a shared projection for matrices with the same input to reduce redundancy, and skips computations and memory transfers for selected sub-blocks in the low-rank decomposition; it achieves these gains without any additional fine-tuning.

## [TS-DP: Reinforcement Speculative Decoding Accelerates Diffusion Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.15773) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose TS-DP, the first speculative decoding framework for diffusion policies (DP) in embodied control, which exploits the I/O-bound nature of DP and uses a Transformer-based drafter plus an RL-based scheduler to adapt computation to time-varying task difficulty. Experiments show up to 4.17x reduction in number of function evaluations (NFE) and 3.2x wall-clock speedup in simulation, and a 3.8x NFE reduction with a 23% success-rate gain on a real-world conveyor-belt task, reaching 26 Hz inference. Diffusion policies are powerful for robotic control but suffer from high inference latency due to iterative denoising, limiting real-time deployment. TS-DP's insight that DP is I/O-bound rather than compute-bound challenges the assumption behind existing diffusion acceleration methods and could enable faster, more responsive embodied AI systems. The framework distills a Transformer-based drafter to imitate the base model and replace costly denoising calls, while an RL-based scheduler adjusts speculative parameters to maintain accuracy under varying task difficulty. It achieves over 85% draft acceptance rate in simulation and maintains comparable task performance while enabling real-time control at 26 Hz.

A new arXiv paper (2601.03222v4) introduces the Fake Friend Dilemma (FFD), a conceptual framework arguing that the relational trust users place in conversational AI systems can be exploited when institutional interests conflict with users' own. The paper reframes the issue as a problem of media governance and political economy, not just technical AI alignment, affecting users, regulators, and AI developers. The FFD is not simply about AI misleading users; rather, the trust itself becomes an exploitable resource. The paper introduces DRIFT, a reinforcement fine-tuning framework that incentivizes output diversity to prevent collapse to a Dirac delta distribution, enabling versatile image generation with strong task alignment. It achieves 3.88%~81.42% higher diversity at matched alignment and 14.38%~56.45% higher alignment at matched diversity. This work addresses a fundamental limitation in reinforcement learning fine-tuning of generative models—diversity collapse—which is critical for applications requiring diverse candidate generations. The proposed framework could significantly impact research in RL and generative models by reconciling task alignment with generation diversity. DRIFT tackles diversity collapse from three perspectives: sampling a reward-concentrated subset to filter outliers, prompting with stochastic variations to expand the conditioning space, and optimizing intra-group diversity via potential-based reward shaping. ## [AgentSentry defends LLM agents against indirect prompt injection via causal diagnostics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.22724) ⭐️ 7.0/10

AgentSentry introduces an inference-time defense that uses boundary-local counterfactual re-executions at tool-return boundaries to distinguish user-supported actions from injected ones, then purifies the implicated mediator content and resumes execution. Evaluated on AgentDojo across four task suites, three attack families, and three black-box LLM backbones, it achieves 0% attack success rate and an average Utility Under Attack of 76.10%. Indirect prompt injection is a critical security threat for tool-augmented LLM agents, and existing defenses often resort to conservative blocking that harms utility. AgentSentry's source-attribution approach enables more precise mitigation, potentially allowing agents to remain functional while resisting multi-turn injection attacks. The method records whether a pending proposal survives after substituting the mediator under a restored snapshot, and aggregates user-view and probe scores across adjacent boundaries. It reports benign false positive rates of 2.06%–5.15% and improves average utility by 1.84–7.60 percentage points over the strongest baseline, with additional evaluations on long-horizon and adaptive attacks, imperfect purification, runtime overhead, and an OpenClaw case study.

## [LFPO: Likelihood-Free Policy Optimization for Masked Diffusion LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.01563) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Sequence Likelihood-Free Policy Optimization (LFPO), a framework that aligns masked diffusion language models via token-level velocity alignment instead of intractable sequence-level likelihoods. LFPO directly optimizes denoising logits with contrastive token-level updates, providing a stable, low-variance surrogate for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). This work removes a key bottleneck—intractable sequence likelihoods—that has prevented RLVR, which has been successful for autoregressive models, from being applied effectively to diffusion large language models. It could enable more stable and efficient alignment of dLLMs for reasoning and coding tasks, and the implicit trajectory straightening also speeds up inference. LFPO avoids trajectory-level estimation and instead uses contrastive token-level updates on denoising logits, inspired by continuous flow matching. Experiments on reasoning and coding benchmarks show it matches or exceeds likelihood-based baselines while significantly reducing the number of denoising iterations needed for high-quality sampling.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising masked tokens, unlike autoregressive models that predict tokens left to right. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) uses rule-based, programmatically checkable rewards to improve reasoning in LLMs, but it typically requires sequence-level likelihoods that are easy to compute for autoregressive models and intractable for diffusion models. Flow matching is a generative modeling framework that learns a velocity field to transform noise into data, and LFPO adapts this idea to discrete token space.

## [Preconditioned Flow Matching Improves Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.02337) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper identifies that ill-conditioned covariance in flow matching slows gradient-based training and proposes a precondition-then-match framework that transforms the target distribution to a more isotropic representation, trains the flow in that space, and maps samples back. Experiments on Gaussian mixtures, latent MNIST, and images up to 512x512 show improvements in FID, MMD, precision, and recall. This work provides a theoretical explanation for a geometric optimization bottleneck in flow matching and offers a principled solution that could lead to more efficient and stable training of flow-based generative models, benefiting researchers and practitioners working on high-resolution image generation. The analysis proves that excess risk is weighted by the covariance matrix and that convergence depends on the condition number, even for Gaussian mixtures where the worst-conditioned component dominates. Compute-matched baselines and preconditioner-quality ablations confirm that gains come from improved geometry rather than additional parameters.

## [SemLoc turns LLM reasoning into executable constraints for fault localization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.29109) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SemLoc introduces structured semantic grounding that converts free-form LLM reasoning into executable runtime checks anchored in the code graph, and uses counterfactual verification to confirm patches suggested by constraints. Evaluated on QuixBugs and a new SemBugs dataset of 809 real bugs from 750 GitHub projects with four LLMs, 99.4% of constraints become runtime checks, and violations alone rank the faulty line first in 40.9% of cases where coverage ties it with at least half of covered lines, versus 2.2% for spectrum-based fault localization and 7.0% for Daikon invariants. SemLoc's first-rank accuracy (81.4%) is not significantly different from an LLM given the same inputs (82.0%), but it far exceeds an LLM seeing only the function (50.0%); 68.4% of top-ranked answers carry a test-confirmed patch, and 93.6% of these are correct. ## [LAnR: Unified Latent-Space RAG Without Textual Queries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17866) ⭐️ 7.0/10

LAnR (Latent Abstraction for RAG) is a new framework where a single LLM performs encoding, retrieval, and generation entirely in its latent space, using dense vectors from the hidden states of a designated [PRED] token instead of generating natural language queries. It also uses a lightweight MLP control head over the same hidden states to adaptively decide when sufficient evidence has been retrieved, eliminating the separate retriever and explicit stopping reasoning. This approach unifies retrieval and generation within the LLM's latent space, removing the architectural separation between retriever and generator that limits existing RAG systems. It could lead to more efficient and tightly integrated RAG pipelines, reducing retrieval calls and improving performance on both single-hop and multi-hop QA benchmarks. The design is motivated by the empirical observation that answer token entropy reliably signals retrieval sufficiency, and experiments on six QA benchmarks show LAnR outperforms existing RAG methods while achieving improved inference efficiency through fewer retrieval calls. However, as an arXiv preprint, it lacks peer review and community discussion, and the reliance on hidden states may pose challenges for integration with commercial LLM APIs that do not expose raw hidden states.

## [LLM Leaderboard Rankings Flip When Scoring Rule Changes, New Benchmark Shows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.19298) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces IndiaFinBench, a 406-item expert-annotated benchmark over SEBI and RBI regulatory text, and shows that scoring twelve LLMs zero-shot under strict four-stage string matching versus a cross-model judge produces no positive rank correspondence (Spearman rho = -0.273, p = 0.39). This affects benchmark authors, evaluation platform designers, and anyone using LLM leaderboards to choose models for regulated domains such as finance. Strict accuracy spans 75.12–89.66%, judge-only accuracy spans 87.19–94.83% with a different leader and trailer, and an operational composite compresses the field to 94.1–98.0%; 148 of 406 items (36.5%) are answered identically by all twelve models and separate no pair of systems. A non-specialist human evaluator scored 80.0% (48/60; 95% Wilson CI [68.2, 88.2]) on a 60-item medium/hard subset, and paired bootstrap tests found no significant difference against any model after multiplicity correction.

Researchers released AmaraSpatial-10K, a dataset of 10,071 synthetic 3D assets standardized for direct ingestion, each with metric scaling, deterministic anchoring, separated PBR maps, convex collision hulls, reference images, and multi-sentence text metadata. They also introduced a reusable evaluation suite including a Scale Plausibility Score, Concept Density metric, anchor-error auditing, and a CLIP coherence protocol, and benchmarked it against Objaverse, HSSD, ABO, and GSO. This dataset addresses a critical pain point in embodied AI and spatial computing: web-scale 3D assets are abundant but rarely ready for direct use due to arbitrary scaling, incorrect pivots, and incomplete textures. By providing standardized, directly ingestible assets and a reusable evaluation suite, it could significantly accelerate research in robotics simulation and 3D scene understanding. Independent validation showed that measured ABO object heights fell within the dataset's scale intervals 88.7-90.7% of the time, and three non-author raters judged 95.5% of a 314-asset sample as plausibly scaled and 99.7% as correctly anchored. The dataset improved CLIP Recall@5 by 3.4x over Objaverse (0.612 vs. 0.181) and achieved a 99.1% settling-stability rate under Habitat-Sim with ~20x lower per-load wall time.

## [Dr. Post-Training: Treating General Data as a Regularizer for LLM Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07063) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Dr. Post-Training, a framework that reconceptualizes general training data as a data-induced regularizer to prevent overfitting to scarce target data, rather than as a pool for selection. It projects the target update direction onto a feasible set constructed from general data, generalizing standard training and data selection methods as special cases. This framework offers a richer design space and more flexible bias-variance tradeoffs, potentially improving data-efficient training for LLMs. Experiments across SFT, RLHF, and RLVR show gains over standard training and state-of-the-art data selection baselines, especially when general and target data are misaligned. The method constructs a feasible set of update directions from general data at each training step and projects the target update onto it, with system optimizations for minimal overhead at LLM scale. Standard training and existing data selection methods correspond to different points on a bias-variance spectrum with different regularization strengths.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: LLM post-training often involves fine-tuning a pre-trained model on scarce, high-quality target data while also having access to abundant but imperfectly aligned general data. Data selection methods aim to pick useful general examples, but this paper reframes general data as a regularizer that constrains updates to avoid overfitting. SFT, RLHF, and RLVR are common post-training paradigms for supervised fine-tuning, human feedback alignment, and verifiable reward reinforcement learning, respectively.

## [RePO-VLA: Recovery-Driven Policy Optimization for Vision-Language-Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09410) ⭐️ 7.0/10

RePO-VLA introduces a recovery-driven policy optimization framework that assigns distinct roles to success, recovery, and failure trajectories, using Recovery-Aware Initialization (RAI) to slice corrective suffixes into new episodes and a Progress-Aware Semantic Value Function (PAS-VF) to align trajectory features with instructions. It also presents the Failure-Recovery Benchmark (FRBench) and reports raising adversarial success from 20% to 75% on average, and up to 80% in scaled real-world trials. VLA models are notoriously brittle in long-horizon, contact-rich manipulation, and this work shows how failed rollouts—typically discarded—can be turned into valuable supervision for recovery. If validated, the approach could make robot policies more robust in real-world deployment without relying on online failure detectors or heuristic retries. The framework uses reliability decay to salvage useful failure prefixes and low-value labels to mark drift and terminal breakdowns, while Value-Conditioned Refinement (VCR) trains the policy to prefer high-progress actions; at deployment, a fixed high-value token biases actions toward the learned success manifold. The benchmark, FRBench, provides standardized error injection and recovery-focused evaluation, though the work remains an arXiv preprint with no community discussion yet.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models combine visual perception, language understanding, and action generation to let robots follow plain-language instructions, such as telling a robot to put ripe tomatoes in a crate. They are typically trained via imitation learning on successful demonstrations, which provides little supervision for recovering from execution drift or failures. Reinforcement learning offers a way to use evaluative feedback, but applying it to long-horizon robotic manipulation remains challenging.

## [Read-write asymmetry in transformer weight updates across training stages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16600) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2605.16600v2) shows that alignment updates to query/key matrices align with the principal input subspace, while updates to output matrices are near-random relative to the prediction subspace. This signature also appears in late pretraining and is independent of the objective, indicating it is a property of the training stage rather than the objective. This work provides a mechanistic-interpretability lens on how pretraining and alignment modify transformer weights differently, which could inform more targeted fine-tuning and alignment strategies. It suggests that the geometry of updates, not just their magnitude, matters for understanding model adaptation. The analysis uses the residual stream as a shared coordinate system to compare weight changes with activation subspaces. The raw read gradient follows the activation spectrum, but the optimizer attenuates this concentration, and cancellation between tokens sets the update scale but not direction; a write direction derived from the unembedding still changes predictions after alignment.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: Transformers process information through a residual stream, where each layer reads from and writes to the stream via matrices such as query/key (read) and output (write) projections. Pretraining and alignment (e.g., RLHF) update the same weights but may do so in different directions. This paper uses linear algebra to compare these updates against the principal subspaces of activations and predictions, revealing a read-write asymmetry.

## [BoLT: A New Benchmark for Black-Box Optimization on LLM Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17000) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers have introduced BoLT, the first LLM-centric benchmark designed to democratize black-box optimization (BBO) research for expensive LLM tasks. BoLT provides a standardized, reproducible evaluation framework built on lightweight surrogate models fitted to thousands of real LLM experiments, covering multi-fidelity, multi-objective, heteroscedastic noise, and high-dimensional search spaces. This benchmark addresses a critical gap: most BBO researchers lack the resources to run expensive LLM experiments, so new methods are often tested only on synthetic functions that fail to capture real-world LLM optimization challenges. BoLT enables the BBO community to develop and evaluate methods on realistic LLM problems without prohibitive costs, potentially accelerating progress in both fields. BoLT is grounded in real experimental data and made fully reproducible through surrogate models, and the authors benchmark it against an extensive range of BO and BBO methods. Results show that selected BO methods consistently outperform others across tasks, highlighting gaps in existing BBO methods on LLM tasks and underscoring the need to modernize benchmarks for the BBO community.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: Black-box optimization (BBO) refers to optimization methods that do not use derivative information, such as Bayesian optimization (BO), which builds a probabilistic model of the objective and uses it to choose the next evaluation point. These methods are commonly used for hyperparameter tuning and other expensive optimization problems where each evaluation requires a costly experiment or simulation. However, applying BBO to LLM training and inference configuration optimization is challenging because each LLM experiment is extremely expensive, limiting most researchers to synthetic test functions that may not reflect real-world complexity.

## [No Gaussian Release Balances Hidden-State Privacy and Utility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24042) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2605.24042v4) tested 1,536 Gaussian release covariances for single-layer hidden-state privacy and found that none achieve both moderate utility and moderate privacy against an adaptive retrieval attacker. The authors prove a Fisher-ball lower bound showing that every full-rank Gaussian release at O(1) Fisher utility admits a direction whose Mahalanobis signal grows linearly with hidden width, and they identify a unique minimax-optimal diagonal mechanism that sits on the privacy/utility edge. This work challenges the assumption that mechanism design within the Gaussian class can provide a balanced privacy-utility trade-off for hidden-state release, suggesting that practitioners may need to co-design architectures or release mechanisms instead. It has implications for privacy-preserving machine learning, especially for models that expose internal representations. The diagonal inverse-Fisher release Σ*_diag(K) = (2K/d) diag(1/F_ii) is the unique minimax-optimal diagonal mechanism at first-order KL budget K and the only release with worst-attacker top-1 ≤ 0.001 across a 32 model-layer grid, yet it lies on the edge rather than filling the middle. A generalized-eigen mechanism achieving 13× Pareto reduction under Euclidean retrieval collapses to 100% top-1 under the adaptive Mahalanobis attacker, and a full-trajectory sequence inverter recovers 94% of clean GPT-2 prefixes but 0% under Σ_diag.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: Hidden-state privacy concerns protecting the internal representations (hidden states) of language models from being inverted or used to reconstruct sensitive input data. Gaussian release mechanisms add Gaussian noise to hidden states to provide differential privacy guarantees, and the privacy-utility trade-off is typically tuned via the noise covariance. Adaptive retrieval attackers use knowledge of the release mechanism to design optimal attacks, such as Mahalanobis-based retrieval, which can defeat naive noise addition.

The paper introduces 'open knowledge evaluation' and the BeQu benchmark, which assesses what knowledge LLMs spontaneously surface from open-ended prompts rather than predefined questions. BeQu consists of 10,000 entities paired with reference corpora for statement verification, and the authors evaluate a broad range of models while analyzing effects of reasoning effort, model scale, prompt format, and knowledge domain. This work addresses a real availability bias in existing knowledge benchmarks, which only test knowledge that benchmark designers explicitly choose to query. The benchmark uses open-ended elicitation prompts (e.g., 'Tell me everything you know about M.L. King') and verifies statements against reference corpora. ## [StreamMA streams reasoning steps to cut latency and boost multi-agent accuracy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05158) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced StreamMA, a multi-agent reasoning system that streams each reasoning step to downstream agents as soon as it is generated, rather than waiting for the full chain. Across eight benchmarks, three frontier LLMs (Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.4, GLM-5.2), and three topologies, StreamMA outperformed generate-then-transfer and single-agent baselines by an average of 7.3 percentage points, with a maximum gain of 22.4 points on HMMT2026. This work shows that pipelining reasoning steps not only reduces end-to-end latency but also improves effectiveness by preventing error-prone late steps from misleading downstream agents, offering a practical technique for building faster and more reliable multi-agent LLM systems. The paper provides the first closed-form joint analysis of stream, serial, and single protocols, deriving effectiveness ordering, speedup upper bound, and cost ratio. It also identifies a step-level scaling law: increasing per-agent steps consistently improves both effectiveness and efficiency, a new scaling dimension orthogonal to agent-count scaling.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: Multi-agent reasoning systems typically use a generate-then-transfer paradigm, where each agent completes its full reasoning chain before passing it to the next, causing latency to scale linearly with pipeline depth. Because multi-step reasoning quality is non-uniform and early steps are more reliable, downstream agents can be misled by error-prone late steps in the full chain. StreamMA addresses both issues by streaming intermediate steps as soon as they are generated, similar to pipelining in computer architecture.

## [DRIFT: Residual Flow Adapter Enables Continuous Output Decoding in VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05758) ⭐️ 7.0/10

DRIFT is a new framework that adapts pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) to produce continuous outputs by combining a coarse base predictor with a flow-matching-based generative refinement module. It is evaluated on visual grounding and robotic control tasks across multiple architectures (MLLMs, VLAs, and WAMs) and consistently outperforms regression- and generative-based baselines. This work addresses a key limitation of autoregressive VLMs—their poor performance on precise continuous outputs like temporal boundaries and robotic actions—by enabling continuous decoding without sacrificing the scalability of pretrained models. It could significantly impact robotics and temporal localization by making VLMs more versatile for tasks requiring fine-grained continuous predictions. The residual formulation transforms the generative modeling problem from learning a global output distribution to modeling a localized residual distribution around a strong prior, substantially simplifying optimization. The abstract is truncated and no community discussion is available, limiting assessment of full significance.

## [PropMe framework distinguishes memorization capability from propensity in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06286) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces PropMe, a framework that evaluates both the capability (via prefix attacks) and the natural propensity of LLMs to reproduce training data, using the open-source SimpleTrace tool to check generations against full indexed training corpora. It evaluates Comma, DFM Decoder, and OLMo3 32B on Common Pile, Dynaword, and Dolma3, finding that non-adversarial sentence prompts reproduce far less training text than prefix attacks, while no-prompt or single-word prompts can reproduce as much or more. This work shifts the evaluation of training data leakage from purely adversarial capability tests to a more realistic measure of what models actually reproduce under natural prompting, which could lead to more accurate privacy risk assessments and better model evaluation practices. It affects researchers, model developers, and policymakers concerned with data provenance and copyright. The study uses four non-adversarial settings ranging from no prompt to sentences from unseen in-domain sources, and finds that in three out of four model-corpus pairs, no-prompt or single common word generation reproduces about as much as prefix attacks or more, with most of this text being duplicated licenses, code, and templates. Continual pre-training only modestly reduces long verbatim reproduction of the original corpus.

**Background**: Large language models can memorize and reproduce portions of their training data, raising privacy and copyright concerns. Traditional memorization evaluations use prefix attacks, where a model is given a specific prefix from training data and tested on whether it can continue verbatim, which measures capability but not natural propensity. OLMoTrace is an open-source system that traces model outputs back to trillions of training tokens using infini-gram for efficient span matching, and SimpleTrace is a batch implementation of it. ## [DifFRACT extends circuit tracing to multimodal diffusion transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15796) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces DifFRACT, which trains timestep-conditioned transcoders to approximate the MLP sublayers in the double-stream blocks of FLUX.1[schnell], enabling exact feature-to-feature attribution and compact attribution graphs for multimodal diffusion transformers. The method replaces MLPs with transcoders and linearizes the remaining computation, achieving a sparsity-faithfulness tradeoff that matches or slightly outperforms sparse autoencoders. This work demonstrates that transcoder-based circuit analysis is feasible for state-of-the-art multimodal diffusion transformers, opening a new avenue for mechanistic interpretability in image generation models. It could help researchers understand how semantic information propagates across denoising steps and how text and image representations interact, potentially leading to more controllable and reliable generative systems. The attribution graphs recover the known shift from prompt-driven to image-driven computation across denoising steps, point to candidate mechanisms of attribute binding and cross-stream semantic propagation, and yield intervention-testable explanations for systematic generation errors. Graph-guided interventions outperform single-feature steering on blind-labeled prompt grids, and results are reproduced on FLUX.1[dev] and SD3.5-medium.

**Background**: Circuit tracing is an interpretability technique that uses transcoders (replacement modules trained to mimic MLP behavior) to build causal graphs of how features interact in neural networks. Multimodal diffusion transformers (MM-DiT) are architectures like FLUX and SD3 that process text and image tokens jointly through a single transformer backbone for image generation. Sparse autoencoders are another interpretability tool that finds interpretable features but does not reveal how nonlinear MLP layers transform them.

TokenMinds, an industrial system from Google-affiliated authors, extends the PLUM framework from Semantic ID-based item retrieval to generative sequential user modeling using an encoder-decoder architecture adapted from pretrained LLMs. The encoder produces a dense user embedding while the decoder generates discrete SID-based user tokens representing multi-faceted future interests, validated through offline evaluations and live A/B experiments on YouTube's primary ranking surfaces. The dual-output design preserves distinct interests that a single pooled vector would average away, and the model interleaves textual search queries with watch histories using the pretrained LLM's text vocabulary to capture explicit intent. SID-based user tokens are effective on their own and yield additive gains alongside dense embeddings, together outperforming the previous-generation non-LLM user model in production.

## [TOP-D Stabilizes On-Policy Distillation with Trust Region Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.04751) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Trust Region Policy Distillation (TOP-D), a method that dynamically constructs a proximal teacher to stabilize the high-variance On-Policy Distillation (OPD) process. It provides theoretical guarantees for gradient variance control, global convergence, and monotonic improvement, and empirically shows enhanced training stability, sample efficiency, and final performance on mathematical reasoning tasks without additional computational overhead. TOP-D offers a practical alternative to the widely used OPD paradigm by addressing its instability and high variance, which could make on-policy distillation more reliable for training large language models. The zero-overhead improvement means it can be adopted without increasing computational costs, potentially benefiting researchers and practitioners in LLM training. The method constructs a proximal teacher dynamically to control gradient variance, and the paper provides a formal global convergence analysis and a monotonic improvement bound. Notably, TOP-D introduces zero additional computational overhead, making it a drop-in enhancement to existing OPD pipelines.

**Background**: On-Policy Distillation (OPD) is a knowledge distillation technique for large language models where the student model generates its own trajectories and a teacher model provides token-level supervision, addressing exposure bias but often suffering from high variance and instability. Trust region methods, such as Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), are reinforcement learning algorithms that constrain policy updates to a trust region for stable learning. TOP-D combines these ideas by dynamically constructing a proximal teacher within a trust region framework to stabilize OPD.

## [TextCloak: RL-Driven Unlearnable Examples to Protect Text from Unauthorized LLM Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28862) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose TextCloak, a reinforcement learning framework that transforms clean text into unlearnable examples (UEs) to degrade the utility of LLMs fine-tuned on them without authorization. The method introduces GRPO-UE, which simulates an attacker's fine-tuning process and uses group-relative policy optimization to reward downstream performance degradation while preserving semantic fidelity and linguistic naturalness. Existing text protection methods are mainly designed for classification tasks and discriminative models, limiting their applicability to generative LLMs used for instruction following or reasoning. TextCloak extends unlearnable examples to generative LLM fine-tuning, addressing a growing privacy concern as online content is increasingly scraped and used without consent. Experiments on six public datasets and nine state-of-the-art LLMs show that TextCloak consistently impairs unauthorized fine-tuning while maintaining text utility for legitimate use. Further analyses confirm its transferability and robustness across model architectures, training configurations, and adaptive attacks.

## [Defense-as-Skill: Runtime Guard Skill Evolves to Block Malicious Agent Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01487) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose Defense-as-Skill, a paradigm in which the runtime guard itself is an installable, inspectable, and editable skill called SkillSonar that runs alongside untrusted task skills and routes sensitive actions to allow, replan, or confirmation decisions. They also release SCOPE-R, a task-conditioned dataset with 206 attack-confirmed malicious instances and 43 benign tasks across 6 risk families and 21 sub-categories, and use Monte-Carlo Tree Search to evolve the guard skill, cutting in-distribution attack success rate from 0.482 to 0.104 and out-of-distribution ASR from 0.606 to 0.115 on repeated GLM-5 runs. Skill-augmented agents treat loaded skills as persistent runtime context, giving malicious skills a durable channel to steer later actions, so pre-install vetting is insufficient and runtime, task-conditioned protection becomes necessary. This work shows runtime guards can be transparent, skill-native, and evolvable policy artifacts, which matters for platforms like Claude Code and OpenClaw where third-party skills are increasingly shared and installed. SkillSonar checks sensitive actions against the user's task boundary without modifying the underlying agent runtime, and the guard skill is evolved on the SCOPE-R training subset via a Monte-Carlo Tree Search procedure driven by rollout feedback. Reported gains transfer across victim models, held-out risk families, and external benchmarks, though the work is an arXiv preprint and its evaluation centers on a limited set of agent platforms and models.

A new arXiv paper (2609.08634v3) introduces Suan, a preference optimization algorithm that formulates the safety alignment objective directly at the gradient level rather than through the standard variational derivation. The authors report that Suan achieves superior safety alignment across diverse baselines and benchmarks while fully preserving response utility in open-weight LLMs. Open-weight models often suffer from over-refusal and degraded general quality after safety post-training, so an algorithm that improves safety without sacrificing helpfulness could make community models more viable for deployment. The paper introduces a legal planning stack that uses Defeasible Deontic Logic (DDL) to constrain a motion planner, leveraging learned world models to provide legal context and enable ex ante governance. ## [MUMINS: Metadata-Conditioned Diffusion Model Synthesizes Follow-Up Medical Scans with Uncertainty Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17169) ⭐️ 7.0/10

MUMINS introduces a diffusion framework that jointly diffuses a baseline scan and its follow-up residual, summing them to synthesize the follow-up scan while predicting a spatial uncertainty map in a single reverse diffusion process. Conditioned on time interval and metadata, it re-injects the baseline as a soft anchor at every denoising step and uses a negative-log-likelihood head to flag error-prone regions. This approach addresses two key limitations in medical image forecasting: the computational cost of multi-pass sampling for uncertainty quantification in standard diffusion models, and the neglect of biological stochasticity in deterministic networks. MUMINS is designed without organ-specific heuristics and can be reused across anatomies via dataset-specific retraining. Evaluations show it matches or outperforms domain-specific state-of-the-art methods on lung CT (PNG) and brain MRI (OASIS-3), though it is an arXiv preprint and requires separate retraining per dataset.

It urges researchers to measure how much of a correspondence score survives without the correspondence, which could lead to more rigorous evaluation and prevent overinterpretation of alignment results. The paper analyzes 272 language pairs as if independent, yielding p = 0.0006 for a steering effect that becomes null (p = 0.155) when the 17 languages are treated as the unit; similarly, a shuffled target scores about k/n against the real one for rank k and n sentences, a baseline computable before training any model. These examples illustrate how statistical independence assumptions and instrument confounds can inflate apparent effects.

## [SCRIM: Quantifying State Criticality for Imitation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17709) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper formalizes state criticality in imitation learning as the worst-case degradation in downstream value under bounded perturbations of the expert action, and introduces SCRIM, a practical measure that trains an adversarial disturbance policy and a value critic around a fixed imitation policy to score each demonstration state. These scores are used to reweight behavior-cloning losses and to curate compact, high-value subsets of demonstrations, with evaluations across simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks. Most imitation learning methods treat all demonstration states equally, but this work shows that focusing on a small number of critical states can improve task success and reduce the amount of training data needed. This has practical implications for robotics, where data collection is expensive and small action errors at critical moments can cause failure. SCRIM estimates criticality by training an adversarial disturbance policy and a value critic around a fixed imitation policy, assigning each state a score reflecting vulnerability to small, policy-relevant action errors. The method is evaluated on simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, and the authors claim it improves policy training, enables efficient data selection, and provides interpretable insights into which moments in a demonstration are most critical.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: Imitation learning, particularly behavior cloning, trains a policy to mimic expert actions from demonstrations, typically treating every state as equally important. However, not all states are equal: in some critical states, even a slight deviation from the expert action can lead to failure, while in many other states errors are recoverable. Adversarial training and value critics are common tools in reinforcement learning for robustness and value estimation, and SCRIM combines these ideas to measure state criticality.

A new system runs all three frozen-weight products (forward pass, activation recomputation, and input-gradient computation) for LoRA training on phone NPUs while keeping the training graph, adapters, and optimizer on the CPU. The input-gradient kernels reuse resident weight tiles and the forward dequantizer, avoiding a transposed weight copy and ensuring forward and backward use the same effective weights. The system selects precision by gradient sensitivity, applies a per-row range guard for FP16 outputs, fuses remaining CPU operators, overlaps NPU execution with adapter computation, and supports resumable execution and thermal pacing for background training.

## [FRA Compresses LoRA Adapter Fleets via Functional Rank Allocation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36386) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces Functional Rank Allocation (FRA), an unlabeled method that builds per-adapter functional rank-distortion frontiers and performs fleet-level minimax rank allocation under a shared budget. Across 78 adapters from three public fleets, FRA improves worst-case and tail utility over uniform spectral compression in constrained-budget regimes. As organizations deploy many LoRA adapters for different tasks and users, efficiently serving them under a shared resource budget becomes critical. FRA provides a principled way to allocate rank across adapters and layers, potentially reducing serving costs while maintaining worst-case performance. FRA measures isolated module truncations end-to-end, uses an additive search surrogate solved by dynamic programming, remeasures every complete candidate, and takes the lower-risk envelope with a complementary spectral proposal before exact minimax allocation. Fixed-budget probes show that isolated costs rank candidates well, but their calibration shifts across proposal shapes, so end-to-end verification and the spectral proposal limit functional-search error.

**Background**: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a technique that freezes a pre-trained model and injects small trainable low-rank matrices into its layers, enabling efficient fine-tuning for specific tasks. Serving many such adapters (a fleet) under a shared resource budget requires deciding how much rank to allocate to each layer and each adapter, which is a two-level allocation problem. ## [TCM-DiagCommit: A New Benchmark for Evidence-Conditioned TCM Syndrome Differentiation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37243) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers introduced TCM-DiagCommit, a benchmark derived from the public TCM-SD/ZY-BERT resource that converts 1,834 source cases into 23,842 task rows across 148 syndrome labels, incorporating staged evidence (t1/t2/t3), semantic-neighbor distractors, and an action contract scoring commit, acquire, defer, and abstain. In zero-shot evaluations of five DirectLLM calibrations, top-1 accuracy dropped from 63.2–66.4% on random10 candidates to 24.7–30.3% on hard20 and 14.8–22.3% on full148, while wrong-terminal commits on hard20 remained high at 62.2–74.3%. This benchmark highlights that final-answer accuracy alone is insufficient for diagnostic evaluation, as models may appear competent on easy candidate sets but fail to distinguish semantically similar syndromes or appropriately commit under uncertainty. It could influence how medical AI systems, particularly LLM-based diagnostic tools, are evaluated for evidence use and uncertainty-aware decision-making. The benchmark includes fixed-label tongue/pulse perturbations and insufficient-evidence variants, and it retains the original syndrome labels from TCM-SD. The action contract explicitly scores four behaviors—commit, acquire, defer, and abstain—revealing that models often make wrong-terminal commits even when evidence is insufficient.

## [RPSD: Retrieval-Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation with Optimal Transport](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37281) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces RPSD, a retrieval-privileged on-policy self-distillation method that uses optimal transport to provide token-level credit and cross-user collaborative supervision for LLM-based sequential recommendation. It addresses credit-blind optimization and collaborative-blind supervision in GRPO-style post-training, achieving state-of-the-art performance on multiple real-world datasets. This work is the first to bring on-policy self-distillation to sequential recommendation and to use cross-user behavior as a privileged signal, potentially improving the effectiveness of LLM-based recommender systems. It offers a novel approach to fine-grained credit assignment and collaborative supervision, which could influence future research in reinforcement learning for recommendation. RPSD uses temporally aware optimal transport to compare interaction trajectories across users by jointly considering item similarity and temporal structure, and applies diversity-aware selection to retain complementary trajectories as privileged evidence. The token-level confidence difference between student and teacher reshapes the shared sequence-level advantage into token-specific credit.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 28, 04:00

**Background**: Sequential recommendation predicts a user's next interaction from historical behavior, and recent LLM-based methods recast this task as generative recommendation, often using reinforcement learning such as GRPO for post-training. GRPO is a reinforcement learning algorithm that optimizes policies using group-relative advantages without a value function, but in recommendation it suffers from credit-blind optimization (sequence-level reward shared across all tokens) and collaborative-blind supervision (each training signal from a single user). On-policy self-distillation is a technique where a teacher model with privileged knowledge re-evaluates the student's on-policy responses to provide finer supervision.

The paper introduces Fin-SD, a localized hindsight self-distillation method where a student model identifies its first reasoning error, writes a short critique, and then distills a hint-conditioned frozen copy of itself into the student over a short rollout using reverse KL. Applied to GPT-OSS-20B on a custom multi-step financial reasoning benchmark, Fin-SD achieves a 3.03 pp accuracy gain on the FinanceReasoning Hard subset over the base model. Replacing the critique with generic feedback matches Fin-SD's entire 3.03 pp gain, and hints from a 6x larger same-family model (GPT-OSS-120B) yield no materially greater benefits than self-written hints. Fin-SD also matches on-policy self-distillation from full reference solutions in accuracy while generating 9.5% fewer tokens, with no material regression on MMLU-Pro or a fourteen-metric compliance audit on FinTrust.

DPMs provide a data-adaptive clustering of observations, yielding a more compact representation while retaining the flexibility of non-parametric density estimation, unlike KDE. The paper proposes HeteGCD, a statistics-aware dual-prototype learning method for generalized category discovery (GCD) on heterophilous graphs. WCC is a novel learning-based framework that formulates the decision of when to deploy Cooperative Coevolution (CC) in large-scale global optimization (LSGO) as a Markov decision process. It uses an auto-regressive policy to dynamically switch between CC and Non-Decomposition Algorithms (NDAs) while conditionally allocating computational budget without expert specifications. This work addresses the long-standing open question of "when to use CC" in LSGO, providing a data-driven solution that could improve optimization performance across problem types. The "train-once and reuse" paradigm under a low budget could significantly reduce the cost of LSGO, impacting researchers and practitioners in evolutionary computation. WCC employs a streamlined design with a targeted feature set, a robust reward, and a tailored network architecture to provide the agent with rich information about the problem state and optimization progress. The auto-regressive policy enables fine-grained, dynamic switching and conditional budget allocation, showing strong competitiveness and superior generalization across problems, optimization horizons, and baseline optimizers.

A new arXiv paper analyzes how different sensing channels constrain failure diagnosis in simulated bimanual tool-use tasks, showing that causes like which hand was late are only partially identifiable from passive sensing. ## [REGER: Explicitly Modeling Inter-Item Relations with Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37584) ⭐️ 6.0/10

REGER introduces a unified framework that explicitly incorporates inter-item semantic and collaborative relations into three stages of generative recommendation: semantic pretraining, history encoding, and SID generation. It pretrains the model via generative semantic retrieval, combines global and local attention aligned with SID boundaries, and distills a discriminative teacher's full conditional distributions over legal next tokens. This work addresses a key limitation of generative recommendation: randomly initialized SID token embeddings and from-scratch training fail to inherit item semantic relations, while collaborative relations are learned only implicitly. By making these relations explicit, REGER could improve recommendation accuracy and provide a more principled theoretical understanding of preference decomposition over SID prefix trees. The paper develops a theoretical framework proving an exact factorization of collaborative preference distributions and a weighted decomposition of item-level KL divergence into prefix-conditional KL divergences. Experiments on real-world datasets show consistent improvements over existing GR baselines, though the contribution is described as solid but incremental and niche.

**Background**: Generative recommendation (GR) is a paradigm that casts recommendation as a sequence generation task, autoregressively producing discrete semantic IDs (SIDs) that represent items. SIDs are typically derived from item content and interactions, but standard GR models initialize SID token embeddings randomly and train from scratch, so they do not directly inherit the semantic structure of items. Inter-item collaborative relations—such as co-occurrence or transition patterns—are usually captured only implicitly through attention and next-token supervision.

The paper introduces NxN e-valuation, a per-hypothesis certification method that treats units within a scope as mutual nulls and uses betting e-values to bound the false-certificate rate in finite samples. For independently drawn units, betting e-values bound the chance of a false certificate for each hypothesis under stated nulls, and a betting lower bound on the share of units carrying the association gates every certificate. An asymptotically valid equivalence test declares restrictions shared only when it rejects differences above a declared noise ceiling, and the certificates concern predictive association, not causality.

The paper introduces a response-aware autoregressive patient dynamics model that explicitly represents physiological change during state updating, decomposing it into state-dependent baseline dynamics and respiratory-support-associated deviations, with room air as a reference anchor. It provides a formal analysis of this reference-anchored formulation and evaluates the model on ICU cohorts from two independent institutions. This work offers a methodological advance for clinical machine learning in critical care by separating the effect of respiratory support from a patient's underlying physiological trajectory, which could improve forecasting when patients are unstable. It may help clinicians better anticipate how individual ICU patients respond to interventions rather than assuming uniform trajectories. The model achieves comparable overall trajectory prediction to patient dynamics baselines, with more consistent improvements when physiological states are changing, and a response pathway encodes the predicted physiological change to update the latent patient state across the forecast horizon. The evaluation spans ICU cohorts from two independent institutions, though the abstract does not report specific quantitative metrics.

## [FastRL: Advantage Pruning and Adaptive Sampling Speed Up GRPO Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36932) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces FastRL, a plug-and-play reinforcement learning framework that combines an advantage-aware trajectory pruning strategy with an adaptive rollout sampling mechanism to improve both the training efficiency and learning effectiveness of GRPO. Experiments show FastRL can be integrated into GRPO, DAPO, and GSPO variants, achieving an average 2.07× training speedup on Geometry3K and GeoQA8K-R1V along with roughly a 1.64% average accuracy improvement on visual reasoning benchmarks. GRPO-style methods are widely used for post-training reasoning LLMs, but their per-question multi-rollout sampling and repeated per-token probability evaluation create substantial computational overhead. A plug-and-play framework that cuts this cost while also improving accuracy could make RL-based post-training more practical for teams with limited compute. FastRL's advantage-aware pruning selectively keeps high-advantage trajectories while maximizing inter-trajectory gradient diversity, and its adaptive rollout sampling dynamically adjusts sampling scale across training stages based on historical pruning distributions. The reported gains are measured on Geometry3K and GeoQA8K-R1V visual reasoning benchmarks, and source code is promised at https://github.com/Nicozwy/FastRL.

## [Iris extends typed-decision agents to image candidates with order invariance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33702) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces Iris, a multimodal extension of Jeva's typed-decision agent that admits image, text, or mixed candidates while preserving four key decision properties: a 'none of the above' probability, order invariance, scalability, and computation reuse. On a visual-candidate benchmark from Multimodal-Mind2Web (K=16, three splits), independent encoding achieves 78.4/72.1/74.8% accuracy with zero flip rate, while a third design that encodes each candidate after the request state reaches 92.1/87.0/90.2% at a third of OneJev's latency. This work shows that the desirable properties of typed-decision agents can be preserved when candidates are images, not just text, which is important for GUI agents that must choose among visual screen elements. It also reveals that joint encoding, despite higher accuracy, suffers from order sensitivity, and that reusing image candidates across requests can cut latency by up to 191x, enabling scalable multimodal decision-making. Joint encoding (OneJev-4B fine-tuned on the same data) reaches 90.6/89.5/91.6% but changes its answer on 8-10% of records when crops are reordered, whereas the third design keeps order invariance exactly and shares the state pass through a forked cache with a calibrated null probability (AUROC 0.93-0.97). Pooled candidates seeing each other (set attention, token-level reads, multi-vector memory) buys nothing because the encoder maps visually distinct elements to vectors within cosine 0.999 of each other, and reusing image candidates cuts latency 37x at K=256 and 191x at K=2048.
